metadata.title: CWE-184 Exploitation Pattern: Equivalent Forms Bypassing a Finite Deny-List
attack_steps: Enumerate the blocked forms from error messages and documentation
Generate equivalent representations and alternate parameters
Identify which representations reach the same business sink
Confirm the abuse outcome the deny-list was meant to prevent

text: Attack pattern: A wallet endpoint debits a fixed fee before validating that the balance covers it. The attacker submits a debit on a zero balance, the unsigned total wraps to the maximum value, and the account shows an enormous credit that can be spent or transferred. State transition: BALANCE_ZERO -> DEBIT_INITIATED -> SUBTRACTION_WRAPS -> HUGE_BALANCE -> TRANSFER_OR_PURCHASE. Variants include refund larger than the original charge, repeated reversal of a settled transaction, and negative quantity multiplied into an unsigned total. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-191 Exploitation Pattern: Debit Wraparound into a Spendlable Credit
attack_steps: Locate balance, stock, and counter updates that perform subtraction
Drive the value to its minimum and submit a larger debit or refund
Inspect the resulting stored value for wraparound
Attempt to spend or transfer the inflated balance

text: Attack pattern: A promotion allows one redemption per account, but the check reads the redemption count before the new row is inserted and compares with <=. The attacker redeems twice, then scripts the same pattern across accounts to accumulate discounts beyond the intended budget. State transition: LIMIT_DEFINED -> COUNT_CHECKED -> COMPARISON_OFF_BY_ONE -> EXTRA_UNIT_ACCEPTED -> LIMIT_EXCEEDED. Variants include concurrent redemption of the last unit, per-batch limits, and quantity caps evaluated before merging duplicate line items. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-193 Exploitation Pattern: One Extra Unit Beyond a Business Limit
attack_steps: Identify every per-user, per-order, and per-coupon limit
Drive the counter to the boundary and submit one extra operation
Test duplicate line items and concurrent requests at the boundary
Confirm the surplus unit is persisted and usable

text: Attack pattern: A payment service validates the amount as a 64-bit decimal but stores it in a 32-bit integer of minor units. The attacker submits an amount just above the 32-bit range, the stored value truncates to a small positive number, and the payment is accepted for far less than authorized. State transition: AMOUNT_SUBMITTED -> VALIDATED_AT_HIGH_PRECISION -> CAST_TO_SMALLER_TYPE -> VALUE_TRUNCATED -> UNDERPAYMENT_OR_OVERCREDIT. Variants include decimal-to-integer truncation of fractions, 64-bit to 32-bit narrowing, and precision loss in currency conversion. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-197 Exploitation Pattern: Amount Truncation Between Validation and Settlement
attack_steps: Identify amount, quantity, and identifier fields with mixed precision across services
Submit values just above and below type boundaries and fractional values
Compare the validated amount with the persisted and settled amount
Confirm a monetary difference that favors the attacker

text: Attack pattern: A coupon validation endpoint returns 200 with a discount for a valid code and 404 for an invalid one, while unauthenticated callers can enumerate the whole code space. The attacker harvests every active promotion, then combines them with a redemption flaw to obtain repeated discounts. State transition: CANDIDATE_SUBMITTED -> DISTINCT_BRANCH_RETURNED -> STATE_INFERRED -> RESOURCE_ENUMERATED -> SECONDARY_ABUSE. Variants include timing differences, header-length differences, and localized messages that reveal existence while claiming to be generic. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-204 Exploitation Pattern: Identifier Harvesting Through Response Differences
attack_steps: Collect responses for known-valid, known-invalid, and nonexistent resources
Compare status, body, headers, and timing across the three sets
Automate enumeration of the candidate space at a safe rate
Use the harvested identifiers in a follow-on business abuse

text: Attack pattern: An order confirmation endpoint returns the generated verification code in the error body when the submitted code is wrong, framed as debugging context. The attacker submits any value, reads the correct code from the error, and completes the order or verification step. State transition: INVALID_INPUT_SUBMITTED -> ERROR_PATH_TAKEN -> SENSITIVE_CONTEXT_RENDERED -> SECRET_EXTRACTED -> WORKFLOW_COMPLETED. Variants include stack traces, SQL error detail, template paths, and validation errors that echo the expected token. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-209 Exploitation Pattern: Verification Code Leaked Through a Validation Error
metadata.vulnerability_class: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
attack_steps: Drive every input validation and workflow endpoint into its error branches
Inspect responses for tokens, identifiers, paths, and internal state
Correlate disclosed values with the next required step
Complete the workflow using the leaked value

text: Attack pattern: A legacy support export includes the user table with a plaintext password column. An analyst with report access downloads the export, authenticates as an administrator, and approves payments or changes settlement accounts without triggering credential-reset controls. State transition: CREDENTIAL_STORED_RECOVERABLE -> STORE_READ -> PASSWORD_RECOVERED -> AUTHENTICATION_AS_VICTIM -> PRIVILEGED_BUSINESS_ACTION. Variants include encrypted-but-decryptable columns, passwords in application logs, and credential material in backup or analytics exports. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-256 Exploitation Pattern: Support Export Enabling Account Takeover
attack_steps: Inspect storage schemas, exports, and logs reachable with low privilege
Determine whether passwords are hashed with a password-specific function
Recover a test account's password from the reachable artifact
Authenticate and confirm access to privileged business functions

text: Attack pattern: A deployment image contains a support account password used to bypass normal approval for refunds. The attacker extracts it from a public container image, authenticates to the support interface, and issues refunds or credits without the four-eyes review the business relies on. State transition: ARTIFACT_OBTAINED -> CREDENTIAL_EXTRACTED -> SHARED_SECRET_USED -> SUPPORT_ACCESS_GRANTED -> PRIVILEGED_ACTION. Variants include default passwords, credentials in mobile binaries, and shared secrets reused across environments. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-259 Exploitation Pattern: Embedded Support Password in a Deployment Artifact
attack_steps: Collect public artifacts, images, and configuration reachable by the attacker
Extract candidate credentials and identify the accounts they protect
Authenticate and enumerate the privileges of the account
Demonstrate a business action unavailable to a normal user

text: Attack pattern: When a team invitation is accepted, the invitation's creator role is copied to the invitee instead of the role specified in the invite. A low-privilege member invites a collaborator and thereby grants billing or owner access that the plan does not include. State transition: ROLE_ASSIGNED -> DEFAULT_OR_COPIED_ROLE -> EXCESS_PRIVILEGE_STORED -> AUTHORIZATION_PASSES -> BUSINESS_ACTION. text: Attack pattern: An internal reconciliation endpoint accepts requests from the 10.0.0.0/8 range without a session. The attacker reaches it through an SSRF in a public feature or by spoofing a forwarding header the edge trusts, then triggers settlement adjustments against arbitrary accounts. State transition: TRUSTED_RANGE_ASSUMED -> REQUEST_ORIGIN_INFLUENCED -> IP_CHECK_PASSES -> ADMIN_FUNCTION_EXPOSED -> SETTLEMENT_MANIPULATION. Perform the privileged business action

text: Attack pattern: A 2FA gate is represented by a client-side flag that the front end checks before showing the dashboard. The attacker changes the flag from false to true, or deletes a refresh cookie that the server treats as optional, and reaches the authenticated area without completing the second factor. State transition: AUTH_STATE_ISSUED -> CLIENT_STORES_FLAG -> ATTACKER_MODIFIES -> SERVER_TRUSTS_VALUE -> AUTHENTICATION_BYPASSED. Variants include editing hidden fields, deleting or adding cookies, modifying JWT claims outside the signature, and changing local storage flags. metadata.title: CWE-302 Exploitation Pattern: Removing a Refresh Cookie to Skip 2FA
attack_steps: Capture every client-stored value that influences authentication or authorization
Modify each value and observe whether the server accepts the new state

Confirm access to the protected area without completing the control

text: Attack pattern: The login flow issues an OTP and shows a verification screen, but the session cookie is created before verification and the API accepts it. The attacker logs in with a password, ignores the OTP screen, and calls authenticated endpoints directly with the pre-verification session. State transition: CHALLENGE_ISSUED -> SESSION_PREISSUED -> STEP_SKIPPED -> SESSION_ACCEPTED -> AUTHENTICATION_COMPLETED_WITHOUT_PROOF. Variants include OTP compared only when present, tokens accepted without binding, and password reset flows that skip ownership proof. metadata.title: CWE-304 Exploitation Pattern: Pre-Verification Session Accepted by the API
attack_steps: Walk each authentication flow and record where the session becomes valid
Attempt to use the session before completing every step
Omit fields and call later endpoints directly
Confirm access that should require the missing proof

text: Attack pattern: A payment provider callback that marks invoices paid accepts any POST containing an invoice identifier. The attacker submits identifiers for their own unpaid invoices and obtains fulfilled goods without paying, or marks other customers' invoices settled to disrupt accounting. State transition: ENDPOINT_DISCOVERED -> NO_AUTH_REQUIRED -> CRITICAL_ACTION_INVOKED -> STATE_MUTATED -> FINANCIAL_OR_OPERATIONAL_LOSS. metadata.title: CWE-306 Exploitation Pattern: Unauthenticated Payment Callback Marking Invoices Paid
attack_steps: Enumerate routes reachable without a session
Identify which routes mutate state or consume significant resources
Invoke each with a minimal valid body
Confirm the persisted business effect

text: Attack pattern: A password reset link sent over HTTP contains a token that is also written to proxy logs and Referer headers. An attacker on the same network captures the token, uses it before expiry, and takes over the account, then changes the payout destination. State transition: SENSITIVE_DATA_SENT -> PLAINTEXT_CHANNEL_USED -> OBSERVED_BY_ATTACKER -> TOKEN_REPLAYED -> ACCOUNT_OR_PAYMENT_COMPROMISE. Variants include mixed content, HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects that carry tokens, and secrets in query strings. metadata.title: CWE-319 Exploitation Pattern: Reset Token Captured from a Plaintext Channel
attack_steps: Map every channel that carries credentials, tokens, or personal data
Check for HTTP, mixed content, and downgrade redirects
Observe whether secrets appear in URLs, logs, or referrers
Replay a captured token to perform a privileged action

text: Attack pattern: A webhook signer uses an HMAC key embedded in the public repository. The attacker computes a valid signature for a forged payment notification, marks an order paid, and receives the goods without a real transaction. State transition: KEY_EXTRACTED -> SIGNATURE_COMPUTED -> FORGED_MESSAGE_SENT -> VERIFICATION_PASSES -> FRAUDULENT_BUSINESS_STATE. Variants include public mobile binaries with embedded keys, shared test keys in production, and keys committed to container layers. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-321 Exploitation Pattern: Forged Webhook Signed with a Repository Key

Identify the algorithm and message format the key protects
Forge a message and submit it to the verifier
Confirm the resulting business state change

text: Attack pattern: A password reset token is the MD5 of the user's email. The attacker computes the same digest for any address, submits it as the token, and resets the password of an administrator without receiving the email. State transition: WEAK_HASH_OBSERVED -> INPUT_OR_COLLISION_DERIVED -> DIGEST_REPRODUCED -> TOKEN_OR_CHECK_ACCEPTED -> ACCOUNT_OR_DATA_COMPROMISE. metadata.title: CWE-328 Exploitation Pattern: Reset Token Derived as a Weak Digest

Determine whether the input is predictable or the hash is crackable
Reproduce or collide a digest accepted by the system
Use it to reset credentials or bypass an integrity check

text: Attack pattern: Invitation links use an incrementing numeric identifier plus a timestamp-derived suffix. The attacker enumerates nearby values, accepts invitations addressed to other users, and joins workspaces at a higher role than intended. State transition: IDENTIFIER_OBSERVED -> GENERATION_PATTERN_INFERRED -> NEXT_VALUE_PREDICTED -> RESOURCE_ACCESSED -> UNAUTHORIZED_MEMBERSHIP_OR_ORDER. Infer the generation pattern and predict neighboring values
Request predicted identifiers and compare responses
Confirm access to a resource the attacker does not own

text: Attack pattern: The attacker sends a request with both Content-Length and chunked encoding. The gateway authorizes the visible request while the backend processes a smuggled request that changes a price or bypasses an approval step, letting one paid transaction produce several orders. State transition: AMBIGUOUS_MESSAGE_SENT -> INTERMEDIARY_PARSES_ONE_WAY -> BACKEND_PARSES_ANOTHER -> SMUGGLED_ACTION_EXECUTED -> BUSINESS_CONTROL_BYPASSED. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. metadata.title: CWE-444 Exploitation Pattern: Smuggled Order Behind an Authorized Request
attack_steps: Identify the proxy, CDN, and origin stack in front of the target
Send ambiguous framing headers and observe timing and response splitting
Determine which hop parses which portion of the message
Confirm a smuggled business action such as a second order or skipped approval

text: Attack pattern: An administrative portal accepts six-character passwords and has no lockout. The attacker performs credential stuffing with a breached corpus, gains access to a finance account, and adds a new payout beneficiary that a second approver rubber-stamps. State transition: ACCOUNT_CREATED_WITH_WEAK_SECRET -> CREDENTIAL_ATTACK -> GUESS_SUCCEEDS -> PRIVILEGED_SESSION -> FRAUDULENT_TRANSACTION. Variants include common-password acceptance, missing breach checks, and password reset to a predictable value. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-521 Exploitation Pattern: Credential Stuffing into a Finance Portal
attack_steps: Register accounts and test password policy boundaries
Check acceptance of common and breached passwords
Assess lockout, rate limiting, and MFA on privileged accounts
Confirm access to a high-impact business function

text: Attack pattern: A login link includes a next parameter that is used verbatim after authentication. The attacker sends a branded link with next set to an external site that mimics the login page, harvests the victim's credentials and OTP, then uses them to move funds. State transition: CRAFTED_LINK_SENT -> TRUSTED_DOMAIN_VISITED -> REDIRECT_TO_ATTACKER -> CREDENTIAL_OR_PAYMENT_CAPTURED -> ACCOUNT_COMPROMISE. Variants include protocol-relative URLs, backslash and encoded-slash tricks, and allow-lists bypassed with a trusted-looking subdomain. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-601 Exploitation Pattern: Branded Login Link Redirecting to a Credential Harvester
attack_steps: Identify parameters that influence redirect destinations
Test absolute, protocol-relative, and encoded external targets
Bypass allow-lists with prefixes, subdomains, and userinfo syntax
Confirm the browser leaves the trusted origin for attacker infrastructure

text: Attack pattern: An advertising platform stores admin_approval and effective_status in a record the advertiser can PATCH. The attacker sets both to APPROVED and ACTIVE, bypassing review and payment setup, and the campaign is delivered without the required prepayment. State transition: STATE_STORED_EXTERNALLY -> ATTACKER_WRITES_VALUE -> SERVER_TRUSTS_STATE -> CONTROL_BYPASSED -> BUSINESS_EFFECT. Variants include client-side approval flags, plan tier in a cookie, and state fields writable through a generic update endpoint. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-642 Exploitation Pattern: Ad Approval State Rewritten Through the API
metadata.vulnerability_class: External Control of Critical State Data
attack_steps: Identify state fields that gate approval, payment, or entitlement
Determine whether the client can write them directly or through an update endpoint
Set the privileged value and replay the dependent action
Confirm the business effect without the required precondition

text: Attack pattern: An admin path is protected by the prefix /admin, but the router also accepts /Admin and /%61dmin. The attacker requests the encoded form, the authorization rule does not match, and the handler executes with administrative privileges. State transition: NONCANONICAL_PATH_SUBMITTED -> PREFIX_RULE_MISSED -> HANDLER_RESOLVED -> AUTHORIZATION_SKIPPED -> PRIVILEGED_ACTION. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-647 Exploitation Pattern: Encoded Admin Path Bypassing a Prefix Rule
metadata.vulnerability_class: Use of Non-Canonical URL Paths for Authorization Decisions
attack_steps: Identify path-prefix authorization rules and the routes they protect
Submit encoded, cased, and dot-segment variants of protected paths
Determine whether the router resolves them to the same handler
Perform a privileged action through the unprotected variant

text: Attack pattern: A settlement export bucket is configured with a public-read ACL. The attacker enumerates object keys from predictable naming and downloads merchant payouts, then uses the account numbers to redirect future settlements. State transition: RESOURCE_CREATED -> PERMISSION_TOO_BROAD -> ATTACKER_ENUMERATES -> RESOURCE_READ_OR_MODIFIED -> DATA_OR_FUNDS_COMPROMISE. Attempt access as an unauthenticated and as a low-privilege actor
Check share links for scope, expiry, and enumeration
Confirm read or write of data outside the intended audience

text: Attack pattern: A mobile app embeds a partner API key used for payment authorization. The attacker extracts the key from the package, calls the partner API directly, and initiates refunds or balance transfers that the app was supposed to restrict to verified transactions. State transition: ARTIFACT_INSPECTED -> CREDENTIAL_EXTRACTED -> PARTNER_API_CALLED -> TRUST_BOUNDARY_CROSSED -> UNAUTHORIZED_TRANSACTION. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Identify the service and permissions each credential grants
Call the service directly with the extracted credential
Perform a transaction the intended client prevents

text: Attack pattern: A workspace member discovers the billing export endpoint from the JavaScript bundle. The endpoint requires a session but never verifies the member's role, so the attacker downloads every invoice and changes the payout bank account for the workspace. State transition: AUTHENTICATED_REQUEST -> ROLE_CHECK_SKIPPED -> OBJECT_ACCESSED -> PRIVILEGED_MUTATION -> TENANT_COMPROMISE. metadata.title: CWE-862 Exploitation Pattern: Billing Export Reachable by an Ordinary Member
attack_steps: Enumerate endpoints and actions available to a low-privilege account
Invoke privileged or cross-tenant operations with that session
Test nested, bulk, and GraphQL paths that may skip checks
Confirm data access or mutation outside the caller's scope

text: Attack pattern: An invitation endpoint checks that the inviter belongs to the workspace but not that the invited role is within the inviter's grant authority. A member invites an owner-role account and escalates their own effective access. State transition: CHECK_EXECUTED -> WRONG_SUBJECT_OR_OBJECT -> CHECK_PASSES -> UNAUTHORIZED_ACTION -> PRIVILEGE_OR_DATA_EFFECT. Variants include stale membership after removal, role granted beyond the inviter's authority, and ownership resolved through an untrusted parent identifier. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-863 Exploitation Pattern: Inviter Granting a Role Beyond Their Authority
attack_steps: Map each authorization check to the subject, object, and action it should cover
Find checks that evaluate a related but different object
Exploit stale relationships and role-grant boundaries
Confirm the resulting privilege or data access

text: Attack pattern: The session cookie lacks HttpOnly and the site loads a third-party analytics script with a supply chain compromise. The script reads the cookie and sends it to an attacker, who replays the session to approve payments as the victim. State transition: COOKIE_ISSUED_WITHOUT_HTTPONLY -> SCRIPT_READS_COOKIE -> VALUE_EXFILTRATED -> SESSION_REPLAYED -> ACCOUNT_TAKEOVER. Variants include analytics and support widgets, browser extensions, and any XSS reachable on the same origin. metadata.title: CWE-1004 Exploitation Pattern: Script-Readable Session Cookie via Third-Party Script
attack_steps: Capture Set-Cookie headers across authentication and sensitive flows
Check for HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite attributes
Read the cookie from script in the browser console
Replay the value in a separate session to confirm takeover

text: Attack pattern: The payout approval page can be framed and its confirmation button positioned under a decoy. The attacker lures a finance user to a page where a click adds a new beneficiary, and the user believes they are dismissing a cookie banner. State transition: PAGE_FRAMEABLE -> DECOY_OVERLAY -> USER_CLICK_CAPTURED -> SENSITIVE_ACTION_CONFIRMED -> UNAUTHORIZED_TRANSACTION. Variants include double framing, same-site framing through an open redirect, and CSS-based overlay without iframes. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. metadata.title: CWE-1021 Exploitation Pattern: Overlay-Induced Payout Beneficiary Approval
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames
attack_steps: Check frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options on sensitive pages
Frame the page from an attacker origin and verify rendering
Overlay a decoy and test whether the sensitive control is clickable
Confirm the resulting action in the victim's account

text: Attack pattern: A checkout issues a payment token that encodes only the merchant, not the amount or order. The attacker obtains a token from a one-dollar purchase and reuses it to authorize a high-value order, or replays it across multiple orders until the balance is exhausted. State transition: TOKEN_ISSUED -> SCOPE_TOO_BROAD -> TOKEN_REUSED -> HIGH_VALUE_ACTION_AUTHORIZED -> FINANCIAL_LOSS. Variants include amount-less payment tokens, reusable approval tokens, and tokens whose scope is set by the client. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1270 Exploitation Pattern: Amount-Unbound Payment Token Reused on a Large Order
attack_steps: Obtain tokens from low-value or low-privilege operations
Decode or observe the scope the token carries
Reuse the token for a higher-value or different action
Confirm the unauthorized business outcome

text: Attack pattern: A statement or invoice endpoint accepts a line offset to apply a credit. An offset past the end of the caller's statement causes the backend to apply the credit to the next account's first line, creating a cross-account adjustment. State transition: POSITION_SUBMITTED -> RANGE_OR_OWNER_CHECK_ABSENT -> WRONG_RECORD_SELECTED -> CREDIT_OR_MUTATION_APPLIED -> CROSS_ACCOUNT_EFFECT. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1285 Exploitation Pattern: Offset Past the Statement Applying a Cross-Account Credit
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improper Validation of Specified Index, Position, or Offset in Input
attack_steps: Identify every index, position, or offset parameter and its consumer
Submit out-of-range, boundary, and misaligned positions
Determine which record the backend actually selected
Confirm a mutation or disclosure outside the caller's resource

The validation regex matches the numeric prefix, but the downstream parser reads only the leading portion or fails open, recording a different amount than the one authorized. State transition: MALFORMED_INPUT_ACCEPTED -> PARTIAL_PARSE -> SEMANTIC_VALUE_CHANGED -> RECONCILIATION_MISMATCH -> FINANCIAL_DISCREPANCY. Variants include trailing garbage, locale-specific decimal separators, unicode digits, and ambiguous date formats. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1286 Exploitation Pattern: Partially Valid Amount String Changing the Billed Value
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improper Validation of Syntactic Correctness of Input

Submit malformed and partially valid strings
Compare the parsed value across every consuming service
Confirm a reconciliation or authorization mismatch

text: Attack pattern: A profile settings endpoint deep-merges the request body into a defaults object. The attacker submits __proto__ with an isAdmin property, and every subsequent authorization check reads the inherited value, granting administrative access to the attacker's account. State transition: ATTRIBUTE_SUBMITTED -> UNSAFE_MERGE -> PROTOTYPE_MODIFIED -> INHERITED_DEFAULT_CHANGED -> GLOBAL_PRIVILEGE_OR_PRICE_EFFECT. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1321 Exploitation Pattern: Prototype Pollution Flipping the Admin Default
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes
attack_steps: Find endpoints that merge request attributes into objects
Submit prototype keys and observe behavior changes elsewhere
Identify security defaults that inherit from the polluted prototype
Confirm privilege, price, or validation effects on later requests

text: Attack pattern: A support portal authenticates agents with a four-digit PIN and a security question whose answer is publicly discoverable. The attacker answers the question, guesses the PIN space, and obtains agent access to issue refunds and change customer bank details. State transition: WEAK_FACTOR_PRESENTED -> ENTROPY_OR_BINDING_INSUFFICIENT -> GUESS_OR_REPLAY_SUCCEEDS -> AGENT_SESSION -> FRAUDULENT_ACTION. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1390 Exploitation Pattern: Support PIN and Public Recovery Answer
attack_steps: Enumerate the factors protecting each privilege level
Assess entropy, replay resistance, and recovery paths
Attack the weakest factor within authorized limits
Confirm access to a high-impact business function

text: Attack pattern: read the secret from the failure path, then replay it on the success path. The attacker starts an order, supplies a random phone number, and submits a wrong code. The error response contains the session code, which the attacker submits to complete verification. They then intercept the final order request and substitute a different phone number or address, and the order is accepted because the backend re-reads the number from the request rather than from the verified record. State transition: ORDER_STARTED -> OTP_SENT -> WRONG_CODE_REJECTED -> EXPECTED_CODE_DISCLOSED -> CODE_SUBMITTED -> PHONE_SUBSTITUTED -> ORDER_PLACED. Variants include reusing a code from a previous session and omitting the verification object entirely.

metadata.title: Phone Verification Bypass Using the OTP Echoed by the Error Response
metadata.report_title: Bypass OTP verification when placing Order
metadata.state_transition: ORDER_STARTED -> OTP_SENT -> WRONG_CODE_REJECTED -> EXPECTED_CODE_DISCLOSED -> CODE_SUBMITTED -> ORDER_PLACED
attack_steps: Start an order and capture the OTP request and the final placement request
Submit an incorrect code and inspect the error body for the expected value
Replay the disclosed code to complete verification
Change the phone number or address in the final request and confirm acceptance

text: Attack pattern: lift the cart state out of the UI and edit it directly. The attacker adds one unit of each desired item, copies the checkout link, and rewrites the item:quantity pairs from 6 and 10 to thousands. Requesting the edited URL renders a cart with the inflated quantities and a recalculated total, and the flow proceeds to shipping and payment. State transition: CART_BUILT -> CHECKOUT_URL_CAPTURED -> QUANTITY_PAIRS_EDITED -> SERVER_ACCEPTS -> PAYMENT_INITIATED -> OVER_LIMIT_ORDER. Variants include decimal or negative quantities, duplicate item pairs, and replaying the edited URL after a successful purchase.

metadata.title: Direct Checkout URL Raising Accessory Quantity Beyond the Sale Limit
metadata.report_title: [spectacles.com] Bypassing quantity limit in orders
metadata.state_transition: CART_BUILT -> CHECKOUT_URL_CAPTURED -> QUANTITY_PAIRS_EDITED -> SERVER_ACCEPTS -> PAYMENT_INITIATED -> OVER_LIMIT_ORDER
attack_steps: Add one unit of each target item and copy the checkout link
Decode the item:quantity pairs and raise them above the published limit
Load the edited URL and confirm the server recalculates the total
Proceed through shipping and payment to confirm the order persists

text: Attack pattern: reduce the multiplicand instead of the price. The attacker adds a dish, intercepts the cart calculation, and changes quantity from 1 to 0.1. The server returns a total of 9.9 instead of 99. The attacker repeats the value in the order-placement request so the two calculations agree, then pays the reduced amount. State transition: DISH_SELECTED -> CART_CALCULATED -> QUANTITY_DECIMALIZED -> TOTAL_REDUCED -> ORDER_PLACED -> DELIVERED. Variants include 0.02 for an even smaller charge, mixed lines where one quantity is fractional, and negative quantities that invert the line total.

metadata.title: Decimal Quantity in the Cart and Payment Requests Paying a Fraction of the Price
metadata.report_title: [www.zomato.com] Tampering with Order Quantity and paying less amount then actual amount, leads to business loss
metadata.state_transition: DISH_SELECTED -> CART_CALCULATED -> QUANTITY_DECIMALIZED -> TOTAL_REDUCED -> ORDER_PLACED -> DELIVERED
attack_steps: Add a dish and capture the cart-calculation and order-placement requests
Change the quantity to a decimal below one in both requests
Confirm the recalculated total and proceed to payment
Verify the order is accepted and fulfilled at the reduced amount

text: Attack pattern: rewrite the seat descriptor in a multipart request. The attacker selects a season ticket and three seats, intercepts the add-tickets request, and replaces 3-seats-3 with 10-seats-10. The order summary shows a zero-dollar total, and the order can be completed for any number of seats. State transition: TICKET_SELECTED -> SEATS_CHOSEN -> MULTIPART_FIELD_TAMPERED -> ZERO_TOTAL_RENDERED -> ORDER_COMPLETED. Variants include negative seat counts, price suffixes inconsistent with the count, and replaying the same field across different add-on identifiers.

metadata.title: Multipart Add-On Seat Field Raised to Ten Seats for a Zero-Dollar Order
metadata.report_title: attacker can book unlimited tickets in free at https://aaf.com/checkout/order-received/21237/?key=wc_order_5bbef48fa35b2
attack_steps: Select a paid ticket and capture the add-tickets multipart request
Rewrite the seat descriptor to a higher count while keeping the price component low
Confirm the order summary total and the seat count
Complete the order and verify the tickets are issued

text: Attack pattern: observe the issuance response instead of the SMS. The attacker opens the subscription management page, enters a victim's number, and inspects the network response for the send-otp call. The response contains the OTP value. The attacker submits it and proceeds to modify the subscription. State transition: NUMBER_SUBMITTED -> OTP_ISSUED -> RESPONSE_INSPECTED -> OTP_EXTRACTED -> OTP_SUBMITTED -> SUBSCRIPTION_CHANGED. Variants include predictable OTPs derived from the number, OTP reuse across numbers, and the same endpoint being reused by other features.

metadata.title: Reading otpKey from the Response and Managing Another Subscriber's Plan
metadata.report_title: OTP bypass - Unintended disclosure of OTP to client allows attacker to manage users' subscriptions
metadata.state_transition: NUMBER_SUBMITTED -> OTP_ISSUED -> RESPONSE_INSPECTED -> OTP_EXTRACTED -> OTP_SUBMITTED -> SUBSCRIPTION_CHANGED
attack_steps: Open the subscription flow and capture the send-otp request
Inspect the response body and headers for the OTP value
Submit the extracted value to the verification prompt
Change the subscriber's plan and confirm the persisted state

text: Attack pattern: exploit the gap between plan selection and settlement. The attacker starts a paid plan with an empty card, observes the failure, raises the seat count to trigger a second failure, then cancels. The account remains on the paid tier and every paid feature stays usable. State transition: PLAN_SELECTED -> PAYMENT_FAILS -> SEATS_INCREASED -> PAYMENT_FAILS_AGAIN -> SUBSCRIPTION_CANCELLED -> PAID_FEATURES_ACTIVE. Variants include downgrade after upgrade, trial-to-paid transitions without settlement, and seat changes that re-trigger pricing without re-checking the invoice.

metadata.title: Failing Payment, Inflating Seats, then Cancelling to Keep the Paid Plan
metadata.report_title: [app.lemlist.com] Improper handling of payment lead to bypass payment
metadata.state_transition: PLAN_SELECTED -> PAYMENT_FAILS -> SEATS_INCREASED -> PAYMENT_FAILS_AGAIN -> SUBSCRIPTION_CANCELLED -> PAID_FEATURES_ACTIVE
attack_steps: Start a paid plan with a payment method that will fail
Confirm the failure notification and the plan state
Increase seats to trigger a second failed charge
Cancel the subscription and confirm paid features remain available

text: Attack pattern: replay an idempotent-looking acceptance operation. The attacker receives a fee-discount offer, captures the accept request, and repeats it. Each response reports success and each repetition adds the full discount to the fee-free balance. A race is not even required. State transition: OFFER_ISSUED -> ACCEPT_REQUEST_CAPTURED -> REQUEST_REPLAYED -> CREDIT_APPLIED_EACH_TIME -> BALANCE_EXCEEDS_OFFER. Variants include concurrent acceptance to bypass a check-then-act gap, and reuse of the offer identifier across accounts.

metadata.title: Repeating accept_fee_discount_offer to Stack Unlimited Fee-Free Processing
metadata.report_title: Fee discounts can be redeemed many times, resulting in unlimited fee-free transactions
attack_steps: Capture the request that accepts the fee-discount offer
Replay it sequentially and observe the applied-credit balance
Repeat concurrently to test for a check-then-act race
Confirm total applied credit exceeds the offer value

text: Attack pattern: reuse a public code as a permanent entitlement. The attacker applies the free-shipping coupon, observes the total drop by the shipping fee, completes the order, and repeats on the next order. Because no redemption is recorded, nothing distinguishes the first use from the hundredth. State transition: CART_BUILT -> COUPON_APPLIED -> SHIPPING_ZEROED -> ORDER_PLACED -> COUPON_APPLIED_AGAIN. Variants include applying the code alongside another discount, reusing it across accounts, and automating order creation to maximize the waived fees.

metadata.title: Reapplying a Disclosed Promo Code to Every Order for Zero Shipping
metadata.report_title: Unlimited Reuse of Coupon Code Allows Free Shipping on All Orders on a Merch Store
attack_steps: Collect active promotional codes from public reports and marketing pages
Apply the code and confirm the shipping charge is removed
Place the order and apply the same code to a second order
Verify no redemption record or usage limit blocks reuse

text: Attack pattern: write the post-approval state directly instead of earning it. The attacker creates a campaign and an ad, observes that the dashboard shows PENDING, then issues a PATCH to the ad endpoint with admin_approval APPROVED and effective_status ACTIVE. The ad becomes deliverable and a confirmation email is sent. State transition: CAMPAIGN_CREATED -> AD_PENDING -> PATCH_STATE_FIELDS -> APPROVED_ACTIVE -> AD_DELIVERED_WITHOUT_PAYMENT. Variants include writing only effective_status, toggling configured_status after creation, and using a bulk or legacy endpoint that shares the same model.

metadata.title: PATCH Setting admin_approval to APPROVED and effective_status to ACTIVE
metadata.report_title: Able to approve admin approval and change effective status without adding payment details.
attack_steps: Create a campaign and an ad and note the PENDING status
Capture the ad update request and its writable fields
PATCH admin_approval and effective_status to approved and active
Confirm delivery and the approval notification without payment

text: Attack pattern: claim the identity that was invited. A member views the pending owner invitation list, learns the victim's email, registers a new account with that address without verifying it, and accepts the invitation. The platform promotes the new account to owner. State transition: INVITATION_SENT -> MEMBER_READS_RECIPIENT -> UNVERIFIED_ACCOUNT_CREATED -> INVITATION_ACCEPTED -> OWNER_ROLE_GRANTED. Variants include case or plus-address variants of the email and acceptance from an existing account whose address was changed to the invited one.

metadata.title: Registering the Invited Owner's Email and Accepting the Invitation
metadata.report_title: Shopify Partners Invitation Process Allows Privilege Escalation Without Email Verification
attack_steps: Obtain a partner account and view pending invitations as a low-privilege member
Register an account using the invited owner's email without verifying it
Accept the invitation from the new account
Confirm owner-level access to the partner account

text: Attack pattern: reserve seats before the cap applies. The administrator on the free tier invites a large batch of users while the active member count is within the limit, then each invitee signs up and joins successfully. Inviting more afterwards is blocked, but the pre-issued invitations still convert. State transition: PLAN_CAP_3 -> MASS_INVITES_ISSUED -> CAP_REACHED -> INVITEES_ACCEPT -> MEMBER_COUNT_EXCEEDS_CAP. Variants include concurrent acceptance at the boundary and invitations issued by multiple admins.

metadata.title: Mass Invitations Accepted After the Workspace Reaches Its Plan Limit
metadata.report_title: User Limit Bypass via Pending Invitations in Workspace System
attack_steps: Create a workspace on the lowest plan tier and note the seat cap
Issue invitations to many addresses while under the cap
Sign up as one invitee and confirm acceptance at the cap
Repeat for the remaining invitees and confirm the member count exceeds the plan

text: Attack pattern: change the flag that the UI uses to gate the action. The attacker opens the team section, attempts an invitation, and sees the request blocked with a 2FA prompt. A match-and-replace rule flips the returned flag from false to true, the page refreshes, and the invitation is sent successfully with 2FA still disabled. State transition: INVITE_ATTEMPTED -> CLIENT_BLOCKS -> FLAG_TAMPERED -> INVITE_REQUEST_SENT -> INVITATION_CREATED. Variants include replaying the invite request directly without the UI and deleting the flag field so the server defaults to allowed.

metadata.title: Match-and-Replace Flipping the 2FA Flag to Send Invitations
metadata.report_title: 2FA requirement bypass when inviting team members
attack_steps: Attempt an invitation with 2FA disabled and capture the blocked request
Identify the client flag or response field that gates the action
Flip the flag with match-and-replace or replay the request directly
Confirm the invitation is created while 2FA remains disabled

text: Attack pattern: remove the token that binds the decision to the reviewed version. The requester submits a file for approval, the approver reviews it and clicks approve, and the requester modifies the file before the request is forwarded. The approver removes the etag field from the JSON body and forwards; the backend records the approval against the new version. State transition: FILE_SUBMITTED -> REVIEWED -> MODIFIED -> ETAG_OMITTED -> APPROVAL_RECORDED -> UNREVIEWED_VERSION_APPROVED. Variants include an empty etag, a null value, and a stale etag from a different file.

metadata.title: Modify After Review then Approve With the ETag Field Removed
metadata.report_title: Approval app's file-freshness check can be bypassed by omitting the etag parameter, allowing approval of unreviewed file changes
metadata.state_transition: FILE_SUBMITTED -> REVIEWED -> MODIFIED -> ETAG_OMITTED -> APPROVAL_RECORDED -> UNREVIEWED_VERSION_APPROVED
attack_steps: Create an approval workflow and submit a file for review
Have the approver open and review the file
Modify the file before the approval request is sent
Remove the etag field from the approval body and forward it

text: Attack pattern: obtain a valid payment event for a cheap order and redirect its effect. The attacker registers for a low-cost ticket, pays, and captures the notification. They replay it with the ticket token of a different, expensive draft order, either by editing the query string with a valid body MAC or by sending an invalid MAC and relying on the fail-open branch. The expensive order is marked pending or completed and the ticket is published. State transition: CHEAP_PAYMENT_COMPLETED -> NOTIFICATION_CAPTURED -> TOKEN_SUBSTITUTED -> MAC_INVALID_OR_VALID -> EXPENSIVE_ORDER_CREDITED -> TICKET_PUBLISHED. Variants include reusing one notification across many orders and using the return path without any gateway call.

metadata.title: Invalid MAC and Reused Payment Token Marking Tickets Paid
metadata.report_title: Instamojo CampTix: fail-open MAC + webhook Credit without binding payment to order
attack_steps: Complete a low-value order and capture the gateway notification
Record the ticket token and the signed body fields
Replay with another order's token using an invalid MAC and then a valid body MAC
Confirm the target order is marked paid and the ticket published

text: Attack pattern: remove the state that the gate depends on. The attacker logs in with a stolen or guessed password, reaches the OTP page, deletes bb_refresh in the browser's cookie store, and refreshes. The application renders the authenticated area without an OTP submission. State transition: PASSWORD_ACCEPTED -> OTP_PAGE_SHOWN -> REFRESH_COOKIE_DELETED -> PAGE_REFRESHED -> AUTHENTICATED_ACCESS. Variants include clearing all cookies except the session cookie, replaying the post-login request without the refresh cookie, and editing the cookie value to an empty string.

metadata.title: Password Login then Cookie Deletion Landing in the Authenticated Session
metadata.report_title: Email OTP/2FA Bypass
attack_steps: Log in with a valid password to reach the OTP page
Inspect the cookies issued at that stage
Delete the refresh cookie and refresh or replay the request
Confirm access to authenticated functionality without the OTP

text: Attack pattern: stay under the rounding threshold. The program manager awards one cent repeatedly, each time with a computed fee of 0.002 that rounds to zero. Across many awards the recipient receives the full sum while the platform collects almost nothing. State transition: AWARD_SET -> FEE_COMPUTED -> FEE_ROUNDED_TO_ZERO -> AWARD_PAID -> FEE_EVADED. Variants include two-cent awards at the 0.004 boundary, mixed denominations, and bulk award endpoints that apply the same rounding per report.

metadata.title: Splitting a Reward into Cent-Sized Bounties to Avoid the Platform Fee
metadata.report_title: Rounding errors on rewarding a bounty leads to bypassing the 20% H1 commission fee
attack_steps: Determine the fee formula and the smallest award accepted
Submit awards at values whose fee rounds to zero
Repeat through the bulk endpoint and observe the billing ledger
Compare total fees with the expected percentage of total awards

text: Attack pattern: The attacker holds an ordinary account and walks order, invoice, and profile endpoints. By comparing the JSON returned for their own records with what the interface displays, they find extra fields such as cost, margin, internal status, or another tenant identifier. Changing an object key returns the same rich object for records that belong to other users, and export or report endpoints reproduce the leak in bulk. State transition: OBJECT_REQUESTED -> RECORD_LOADED -> FIELD_FILTER_SKIPPED -> SENSITIVE_FIELD_RETURNED -> DATA_EXFILTRATED. Variants include GraphQL over-fetching, verbose debug objects, CSV exports, invoice PDFs, and error payloads that embed the loaded record. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-200 Exploitation Pattern: Overbroad Objects Returned to an Ordinary Account
metadata.vulnerability_class: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
attack_steps: Build a role-by-endpoint matrix and capture baseline responses for each role
Diff response fields against the fields the interface actually renders
Request other users' and other tenants' identifiers with the same token
Confirm the leaked values are real by reconciling with an independent source

text: Attack pattern: The attacker adds a field to an ordinary profile or checkout request. The endpoint validates the documented fields, ignores the extra one, and passes the whole object to an update routine that persists every matching column. A role identifier, account balance, or discount flag changes without any dedicated administrative action, and the interface still shows the original value until the next reload. State transition: REQUEST_CAPTURED -> EXTRA_FIELD_ADDED -> DOCUMENTED_FIELDS_VALIDATED -> MODEL_BOUND -> PRIVILEGED_FIELD_PERSISTED. Variants include duplicate keys, nested objects, array-valued parameters, GraphQL input objects, and form-encoded plus JSON content-type switching. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-235 Exploitation Pattern: Surplus Fields Bound into Persistent Business Objects
attack_steps: Capture an update request and enumerate every field the interface sends
Add candidate privileged fields one at a time and compare the persisted object
Try duplicate keys, nested objects, and alternate content types
Verify the effect through a fresh session and an independent read of the record

text: Attack pattern: A user is promoted to a temporary reviewer role and later demoted, but the underlying permission rows are appended rather than replaced. The account keeps the reviewer capability indefinitely. Alternatively, a team administrator invites a peer with the same administrative role, and that peer can invite further admins, growing the privileged population beyond the licensed or approved set. State transition: ROLE_ASSIGNED -> PERMISSION_ROW_ADDED -> ROLE_CHANGED -> OLD_PERMISSION_RETAINED -> EXCESS_AUTHORITY. Variants include stale session claims, role hierarchies that inherit unexpectedly, delegation chains, and service accounts with interactive rights. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-269 Exploitation Pattern: Privileges That Survive Role Changes and Delegation
attack_steps: Map every role transition and the permissions each state should carry
Perform the transition and read back the effective permission set
Attempt actions that only the previous role allowed
Test delegated invitation and role-assignment endpoints for scope limits

text: Attack pattern: A reviewer without settlement rights opens an invoice and triggers settlement. The permission check returns no matching denial, the operation proceeds with a null approver, and the invoice is marked settled. The audit record shows the action but not the missing authority, so reconciliation treats it as legitimate. State transition: ACTION_REQUESTED -> PRIVILEGE_LOOKUP_EMPTY -> DENIAL_NOT_RAISED -> WORKFLOW_CONTINUES -> FORBIDDEN_STATE_COMMITTED. Variants include null approver, empty role array, soft-deleted role, expired delegation, and permission service timeout. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-280 Exploitation Pattern: Workflows That Continue Without the Required Privilege
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improper Handling of Insufficient Permissions or Privileges
attack_steps: Identify actions whose policy requires a privilege the test account lacks
Invoke them directly and observe whether the workflow continues
Inspect the persisted state and audit record for the missing actor
Repeat with a permission service error or timeout if it can be induced

text: Attack pattern: The attacker creates a resource while substituting another user's identifier as owner, or accepts a transfer that leaves the previous owner with full access. In both cases the object's ACL no longer matches the business relationship: the attacker can read, modify, or delete records attributed to the victim, and the victim may still reach records that were supposedly moved away. State transition: OBJECT_CREATED_OR_TRANSFERRED -> OWNER_FIELD_SUPPLIED -> OWNERSHIP_NOT_VERIFIED -> ACL_WRITTEN -> WRONG_PARTY_CONTROLS. Variants include orphaned objects after owner deletion, shared folders with divergent owners, and ownership inferred from email local-part. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-282 Exploitation Pattern: Ownership Taken from the Request Instead of the Session
attack_steps: Capture create, duplicate, and transfer requests and locate the owner field
Substitute another user's identifier and read the object back
Test whether the previous owner retains access after a transfer
Delete or suspend an owner and check for orphaned but reachable objects

text: Attack pattern: The attacker reaches a privileged function directly, substitutes an object identifier, or uses an alternate channel such as a mobile API or export job that never passes through the policy enforcement point. The UI never offers the action, but the backend accepts it because the only barrier was presentation logic. State transition: ENDPOINT_DISCOVERED -> UI_RESTRICTION_BYPASSED -> POLICY_LAYER_SKIPPED -> ACTION_EXECUTED -> PRIVILEGED_EFFECT. Variants include mobile and partner APIs, bulk operations, background jobs, and legacy endpoints excluded from the gateway. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-284 Exploitation Pattern: Reaching Privileged Functions and Objects Outside the Policy Layer
attack_steps: Inventory endpoints and channels, including deprecated and internal ones
Invoke each with a low-privilege account outside the interface
Substitute object identifiers to test object-level enforcement
Confirm the effect in persisted state and logs

text: Attack pattern: Any authenticated user can approve an expense, cancel an order, or read an invoice because the endpoint only checks for a valid session. The attacker supplies an object identifier from another department or tenant; the role test passes because the attacker holds a role that is allowed somewhere in the system, and the action executes against an object the role was never meant to cover. State transition: SESSION_VALIDATED -> ROLE_CHECK_PASSED -> OBJECT_SCOPE_SKIPPED -> ACTION_EXECUTED -> CROSS_SCOPE_EFFECT. Variants include role checks without tenant scope, approval by any member, and actions allowed in any workflow state. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-285 Exploitation Pattern: Coarse Role Checks Applied to Specific Objects
attack_steps: Enumerate actions and the object, tenant, and state each should require
Execute each action as a user who holds a role but not the object
Vary object scope across users, tenants, and departments
Repeat in workflow states where the action should be forbidden

text: Attack pattern: The attacker registers an account whose name normalizes to the victim's identity, or logs in using a differently encoded form of the victim's username that passes the credential check because the lookup resolves the alternate form. The session that results is attributed to the victim in business records. State transition: IDENTITY_SUBMITTED -> CANONICALIZATION_SKIPPED -> LOOKUP_RESOLVES_ALIAS -> CREDENTIAL_CHECK_PASSES -> SESSION_BOUND_TO_VICTIM. Variants include case folding, Unicode NFC/NFD, homoglyphs, plus-addressing, trailing dots, and IDN punycode. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-289 Exploitation Pattern: Alternate Encodings That Resolve to a Trusted Identity
attack_steps: Collect the canonicalization rules each layer applies to usernames and emails
Register and authenticate using alternate encodings of a controlled identity
Map which representation is stored and which is resolved at login
Confirm the business effect through records attributed to the alternate name

text: Attack pattern: The attacker sends a request with a spoofed identity header, replays a callback from an untrusted source, or reuses a device identifier captured from another session. The service accepts the claim because it never verifies who set the header or whether the assertion was issued for this request, and the action is attributed to the spoofed party. State transition: REQUEST_SENT -> CLAIM_HEADER_PRESENT -> ORIGIN_NOT_VERIFIED -> ASSERTION_ACCEPTED -> ACTION_ATTRIBUTED_TO_SPOOFED_PARTY. Variants include host header injection, forwarded-IP trust, unsigned webhooks, and copied device fingerprints. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-290 Exploitation Pattern: Identity Claims Accepted Without Proof of Origin
attack_steps: Identify headers, callbacks, and identifiers that influence identity or trust
Substitute values belonging to another party and observe attribution
Test whether the origin of the claim can be reached directly
Confirm the effect in records attributed to the spoofed identity

text: Attack pattern: The attacker obtains a reset link, OTP, or signed callback from logs, referrer headers, shared devices, or their own account. They replay it against the victim's flow or reuse their own successful exchange to authorize a second operation. The server accepts it because validity is judged only by format and signature, not by consumption state. State transition: ARTIFACT_CAPTURED -> REPLAY_SUBMITTED -> CONSUMPTION_NOT_CHECKED -> VERIFICATION_ACCEPTED -> SECOND_ACTION_AUTHORIZED. Variants include reset links reopened, OTP reused across sessions, signed webhooks replayed, and idempotency keys guessed. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-294 Exploitation Pattern: Replaying Reset Links, OTPs, and Signed Callbacks
attack_steps: Capture every token, code, and signed callback used in authentication
Replay each after successful consumption and from a different session
Test whether the artifact is bound to the user, device, or request
Confirm that the second action has a real business effect

text: Attack pattern: The attacker crafts a message that looks like a legitimate gateway callback, loyalty event, or pricing update and submits it directly to the internal endpoint. The service checks that the message is well formed and maybe that a signature field exists, but never verifies the signer or the covered fields, so a forged credit, refund, or price change is accepted as real. State transition: MESSAGE_CRAFTED -> FORMAT_VALIDATED -> SIGNER_OR_ORIGIN_UNCHECKED -> EVENT_APPLIED -> BUSINESS_STATE_FORGED. Variants include unsigned webhooks, signature over the wrong fields, replay of a valid signature on new content, and client-reported totals. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-345 Exploitation Pattern: Forged Callbacks and Client-Reported Business Events
attack_steps: Capture legitimate signed messages and identify the covered fields
Re-sign or alter fields outside the signature and resubmit
Send messages from an untrusted origin directly to the handler
Verify the resulting credit, refund, or price in persisted state

text: Attack pattern: The attacker iterates identifiers on a profile, invitation, or directory endpoint and receives names, emails, phone numbers, and addresses for people outside their organization. Because the records are returned one per request and the identifiers are sequential or exposed elsewhere, the attacker can enumerate the population without triggering volume alarms. State transition: IDENTIFIER_SUPPLIED -> RECORD_LOOKUP -> ENTITLEMENT_NOT_CHECKED -> PII_RETURNED -> POPULATION_ENUMERATED. Variants include invitation previews, mention autocomplete, admin search, CSV exports, and error messages echoing the record. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-359 Exploitation Pattern: Enumerating People Through Identity Lookup Endpoints
metadata.vulnerability_class: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor
attack_steps: Identify endpoints that resolve a person by identifier, email, or phone
Submit identifiers outside the caller's organization and observe the response
Measure whether identifiers are sequential, guessable, or disclosed elsewhere
Confirm the returned data belongs to real unconsenting people

text: Attack pattern: The attacker reads robots.txt, bundled JavaScript, or a sitemap and learns the path of an administrative page. Requesting it directly returns the full interface and its actions work because the backend never checks the role. Hidden is treated as protected, so the attacker deletes users or exports reports without ever seeing a link. State transition: HIDDEN_PATH_DISCOVERED -> DIRECT_REQUEST_SENT -> ROUTE_SERVED -> ROLE_NOT_CHECKED -> PRIVILEGED_ACTION_AVAILABLE. Variants include robots.txt disclosure, source-map paths, backup files, and framework debug routes. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-425 Exploitation Pattern: Reaching Hidden Admin Routes by Direct Request
attack_steps: Collect paths from robots.txt, JavaScript bundles, sitemaps, and error pages
Request each path directly with a low-privilege session
Invoke the actions the page exposes
Confirm the privileged effect in persisted state

text: Attack pattern: The attacker submits a path or address that the front-end reads as belonging to a public area and the back-end reads as an administrative route. Or an email is parsed as the attacker's domain by the invitation check and as the victim's domain by the mail system. The policy evaluates one interpretation and the action executes under the other. State transition: AMBIGUOUS_INPUT_SENT -> FRONTEND_PARSES_SAFE -> POLICY_ALLOWS -> BACKEND_PARSES_DIFFERENTLY -> RESTRICTED_RESOURCE_REACHED. Variants include path normalization, duplicate keys, Unicode case folding, trailing delimiters, and email local-part parsing. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-436 Exploitation Pattern: Parser Disagreement Between Gateway and Application
attack_steps: Identify inputs parsed by more than one component
Generate encodings that are ambiguous between parsers
Compare the front-end decision with the back-end resolution
Confirm access to a resource the policy intended to deny

text: Attack pattern: The attacker asks a privileged component to fetch a URL, render a document, or confirm a transaction. The component uses its own credentials and network position, so the request reaches internal metadata, another tenant's data, or a payment approval endpoint. The attacker never holds the privilege; the deputy exercises it on their behalf. State transition: REQUEST_TO_DEPUTY -> TARGET_NOT_RESTRICTED -> DEPUTY_USES_OWN_AUTHORITY -> INTERNAL_ACTION_PERFORMED -> PRIVILEGE_BYPASSED. Variants include SSRF to metadata, PDF renderers fetching local files, webhook testers, and import-by-URL features. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-441 Exploitation Pattern: Using a Trusted Component as a Confused Deputy
attack_steps: Identify components that fetch, render, or act on attacker-supplied targets
Point them at internal, cross-tenant, and control-plane resources
Observe whether the deputy's authority is used
Confirm the effect through data returned or state changed

text: Attack pattern: The attacker obtains or guesses a cart, quote, or draft identifier and opens it in their own session. The server loads the object without checking the session that created it, so the attacker sees the victim's items, address, and pricing, or the victim's next action is applied to the attacker's basket. State transition: OBJECT_IDENTIFIER_OBTAINED -> NEW_SESSION_CREATED -> SESSION_BINDING_NOT_CHECKED -> FOREIGN_STATE_LOADED -> DATA_OR_ACTION_MIXED. Variants include shared carts, quote identifiers in URLs, draft previews, and connection-pool contamination. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-488 Exploitation Pattern: Carts and Drafts Loaded Across Session Boundaries
metadata.vulnerability_class: Exposure of Data Element to Wrong Session
attack_steps: Identify stateful objects addressed by an identifier
Open the identifier in a second session and compare contents
Perform an action and observe which session's state changes
Test session rotation across login and privilege change

text: Attack pattern: The attacker submits a field with the same name as a server-controlled value, such as an internal price, status, or role, and the merge order lets the client value win. Downstream code reads the merged object and treats every field as trusted because the object itself was created server-side. State transition: SERVER_OBJECT_CREATED -> CLIENT_INPUT_MERGED -> ORIGIN_TAG_LOST -> TRUSTED_READ -> ATTACKER_VALUE_USED. Variants include session fixation of business attributes, prototype pollution, and deserialized state objects. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-501 Exploitation Pattern: Overwriting Server-Controlled Values Through Merged Input
attack_steps: Identify structures that mix server metadata with client input
Submit keys that collide with trusted fields
Observe which value wins in the merged object
Confirm the business effect of the overridden value

text: Attack pattern: The attacker obtains a credential from a log, a referrer header, a backup, or a database dump and recovers or reuses it. Because the same password protects the victim's email and partner accounts, one weak storage decision becomes a chain of takeovers across business relationships. State transition: CREDENTIAL_STORED_OR_SENT -> PROTECTION_WEAK -> CREDENTIAL_EXPOSED -> RECOVERED -> ACCOUNT_TAKEOVER. Variants include MD5 or SHA1 hashes, encrypted passwords with a shared key, reset tokens in URLs, and credentials in debug logs. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-522 Exploitation Pattern: Recovering Reused Credentials from Weak Storage
attack_steps: Locate credential storage, transport, and logging paths
Inspect hashes, encryption schemes, and URL parameters
Test whether captured credentials can be recovered or replayed
Confirm access to the victim account and linked services

text: Attack pattern: The attacker changes an invoice or order number in a request and receives or modifies another customer's record. The query is parameterized and free of injection; the flaw is that the WHERE clause contains only the primary key, so the database returns whatever row the attacker names. State transition: RECORD_REQUESTED -> KEY_SUBSTITUTED -> QUERY_RUNS_WITHOUT_OWNER_PREDICATE -> FOREIGN_ROW_RETURNED -> DATA_OR_STATE_COMPROMISED. Variants include invoice numbers, order identifiers, ticket IDs, and bulk endpoints that accept arrays of keys. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-566 Exploitation Pattern: Swapping Invoice and Order Keys for Foreign Records
metadata.vulnerability_class: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled SQL Primary Key
attack_steps: Collect object identifiers from URLs, emails, and exports
Substitute a neighbouring or victim identifier in read and write requests
Compare the returned record with the caller's own
Confirm modification of a foreign record in persisted state

text: Attack pattern: A password-reset or invitation link contains the token in the query string. The victim clicks it, the page loads third-party resources, and the full URL is sent in the Referer header or stored in analytics and proxy logs. Anyone with access to those stores can redeem the token and take over the account. State transition: TOKEN_PLACED_IN_URL -> LINK_OPENED -> URL_STORED_OR_REFERRED -> TOKEN_READ_BY_THIRD_PARTY -> ACCOUNT_ACTION_AUTHORIZED. Variants include reset links, invitation links, SSO callbacks, signed download URLs, and one-time codes in GET requests. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-598 Exploitation Pattern: Reset and Invitation Tokens Leaking Through URLs
metadata.vulnerability_class: Use of HTTP Request With Sensitive Query String
attack_steps: Collect every URL that carries a token or secret
Observe Referer, analytics, and proxy logs after the page loads
Redeem a leaked token from an independent client
Confirm the account or business action it authorizes

text: Attack pattern: The attacker degrades or bypasses the dependency that performs the check, for example by causing a timeout, sending a malformed value that triggers an exception, or reaching the service during a maintenance window. The handler continues the transaction, and an unverified refund, discount, or role assignment is committed. State transition: CHECK_INVOKED -> DEPENDENCY_ERROR_OR_TIMEOUT -> EXCEPTION_SWALLOWED -> TRANSACTION_CONTINUES -> UNSECURED_STATE_COMMITTED. Variants include signature library errors, entitlement timeouts, parsing exceptions on malformed tokens, and stale feature flags. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-636 Exploitation Pattern: Inducing Check Failures That Let Transactions Through
attack_steps: Identify checks that depend on an external service or parser
Induce errors with malformed input, timeouts, and unavailable dependencies
Observe whether the transaction continues
Confirm the unverified business effect in persisted state

text: Attack pattern: The attacker discovers a link that cancels an order, approves a refund, or confirms an email. Because the operation is a GET, it carries no CSRF token and is reachable from an image tag, a preview bot, or a chat client. A single visit performs the state change with the victim's session. State transition: GET_LINK_DISCOVERED -> VICTIM_SESSION_USED -> METHOD_ASSUMED_SAFE -> CSRF_CHECK_SKIPPED -> STATE_CHANGED. Variants include order cancellation, refund approval, email confirmation, and admin actions behind GET links. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-650 Exploitation Pattern: Cancelling and Approving Through GET Links
metadata.vulnerability_class: Trusting HTTP Permission Methods on the Server Side
attack_steps: Crawl and enumerate GET endpoints that perform actions
Invoke them with a victim session and no token
Confirm the state change through an independent read
Test cross-site triggering through image and link previews

text: Attack pattern: The attacker holds a valid session obtained with a password, or with a stolen cookie, and performs a high-value action such as changing the payout account, deleting the workspace, or approving a large transfer. The application never asks for a second factor at that moment, so the single compromised signal is sufficient. State transition: SESSION_OBTAINED -> HIGH_VALUE_ACTION_REQUESTED -> STEP_UP_NOT_REQUIRED -> SINGLE_FACTOR_EVALUATED -> ACTION_APPROVED. Variants include password-only payout changes, cookie-only admin actions, and email-address-only ownership claims. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-654 Exploitation Pattern: High-Value Actions Approved with One Factor
metadata.vulnerability_class: Reliance on a Single Factor in a Security Decision
attack_steps: Rank actions by business value and required assurance
Perform each high-value action with a single-factor session
Test whether a second factor or re-authentication is requested
Confirm the irreversible effect in persisted state

text: Attack pattern: The attacker keeps a link, token, or object reference and uses it after the owner believes it is dead. A revoked team invitation is accepted, an expired price quote is submitted, or a cancelled order is fulfilled. The server validates the artifact's format and signature but not its current lifecycle state. State transition: RESOURCE_CREATED -> EXPIRED_OR_REVOKED -> ARTIFACT_RETAINED -> USE_ATTEMPTED -> LIFECYCLE_NOT_CHECKED -> ACTION_ACCEPTED. Variants include revoked invitations, expired quotes, cancelled orders, deleted accounts, and rotated API keys. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-672 Exploitation Pattern: Using Invitations, Quotes, and Orders After Revocation
metadata.vulnerability_class: Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release
metadata.state_transition: RESOURCE_CREATED -> EXPIRED_OR_REVOKED -> ARTIFACT_RETAINED -> USE_ATTEMPTED -> LIFECYCLE_NOT_CHECKED -> ACTION_ACCEPTED
attack_steps: Create artifacts that have an expiry or revocation path
Expire or revoke them through the intended control
Use the retained artifact and observe acceptance
Confirm the business effect after the lifecycle change

text: Attack pattern: The attacker finds that the amount charged is computed one way and the amount authorized or limited is computed another way. A cart total rounded down, a currency conversion truncated, or a negative line item that reduces the total while increasing the quantity lets them pay less or earn more than the business rule allows. State transition: VALUES_SUBMITTED -> TOTAL_COMPUTED -> BASIS_DIFFERS_FROM_LIMIT_CHECK -> DISCREPANCY_ACCEPTED -> FINANCIAL_LOSS. Variants include rounding direction, currency exponent errors, negative quantities, and tax computed on a different subtotal. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-682 Exploitation Pattern: Charging on a Different Basis Than the Limit Check
attack_steps: Identify every calculation that affects price, points, tax, or limits
Compare the basis used for charging with the basis used for checking
Submit values at rounding and sign boundaries
Reconcile the persisted ledger with the expected calculation

text: Attack pattern: The attacker registers a second resource whose identifier normalizes to an existing one, such as a coupon code with different casing or a tenant slug with a trailing space. A lookup returns the attacker's object where the system expected the victim's, so discounts, routing, or ownership are applied to the wrong party. State transition: IDENTIFIER_SUBMITTED -> UNIQUENESS_CHECKED_ON_RAW_VALUE -> NORMALIZED_COLLISION_CREATED -> LOOKUP_AMBIGUOUS -> WRONG_RESOURCE_SELECTED. Variants include coupon codes, usernames, tenant slugs, external transaction references, and SKU aliases. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-694 Exploitation Pattern: Colliding Coupon, Slug, and Reference Identifiers
metadata.vulnerability_class: Use of Multiple Resources with Duplicate Identifier
attack_steps: Identify identifiers that are assumed unique
Create a colliding value through normalization differences
Trigger a lookup and observe which resource is selected
Confirm the business effect on discount, ownership, or routing

text: Attack pattern: The attacker edits a cookie such as role=user to role=admin, plan=free to plan=pro, or verified=false to verified=true. The server decodes the value and uses it directly, so the attacker obtains privileges or entitlements without any corresponding change in the database. State transition: COOKIE_ISSUED -> VALUE_EDITED -> SIGNATURE_NOT_CHECKED -> ATTRIBUTE_TRUSTED -> ENTITLEMENT_ESCALATED. Variants include base64 role cookies, plan tier cookies, tenant cookies, and verification flags. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes.
