Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-784 Exploitation Pattern: Editing Role and Plan Cookies
metadata.vulnerability_class: Reliance on Cookies without Validation and Integrity Checking in a Security Decision
attack_steps: Inventory cookies that influence authorization or entitlement
Decode, edit, and re-encode each value
Send the modified cookie and observe the decision
Confirm the entitlement or privilege effect in server-side state

text: Attack pattern: The attacker creates a workspace, project, or integration and receives a default configuration that is more permissive than the business permits: public visibility, an unexpiring token, or unsigned callbacks. The attacker does not need to exploit a bug; they simply use what provisioning gave them and the exposure persists until someone notices. State transition: RESOURCE_CREATED -> DEFAULT_APPLIED -> HARDENING_NOT_REQUIRED -> PERMISSIVE_STATE_PERSISTS -> UNAUTHORIZED_ACCESS_OR_COST. Variants include public-by-default projects, non-expiring keys, trial entitlements, and open webhook receivers. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1188 Exploitation Pattern: Permissive Defaults in Provisioned Resources
metadata.vulnerability_class: Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default
attack_steps: Create each resource type with a fresh account
Inspect visibility, sharing, token lifetime, and callback verification defaults
Attempt access from an unrelated account or unsigned source
Confirm the default state persists without an explicit hardening step

text: Attack pattern: A user with a read-only reporting role discovers that the same permission also permits export of raw customer records. Or a project member can edit approved invoices because the permission covers the whole invoice module. The policy is not missing; it simply cannot distinguish the action the attacker performs from the one they were granted. State transition: COARSE_PERMISSION_GRANTED -> FINE_ACTION_REQUESTED -> SCOPE_NOT_DISTINGUISHED -> ACTION_ALLOWED -> POLICY_INTENT_BROKEN. Variants include read versus export, draft versus approved, project versus tenant, and view versus impersonate. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1220 Exploitation Pattern: Using a Broad Grant for a Fine-Grained Action
attack_steps: Decompose each module into operations, objects, and states
Map the actual permission scope to that decomposition
Perform actions that share the permission but exceed its intent
Confirm the effect on records or data outside the intended scope

text: Attack pattern: The attacker cannot open a restricted document but can search for it, list its versions, or request a thumbnail. The metadata endpoint returns the title, owner, modification time, and sometimes extracted text. By querying candidate terms, the attacker confirms the existence and contents of confidential records one fragment at a time. State transition: DIRECT_ACCESS_DENIED -> METADATA_ENDPOINT_REACHED -> ACL_NOT_INHERITED -> TITLE_OR_SNIPPET_RETURNED -> CONTENT_INFERRED. Variants include search snippets, thumbnails, version history, audit logs, and pre-signed URL parameters. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1230 Exploitation Pattern: Inferring Restricted Content from Search and Previews
metadata.vulnerability_class: Exposure of Sensitive Information Through Metadata
attack_steps: Identify metadata surfaces for restricted resources
Query them with candidate terms and identifiers
Compare metadata returned with the direct-access denial
Reconstruct enough content to demonstrate the leak

text: Attack pattern: The attacker triggers a change in one representation and immediately acts on another. They cancel an order in the order service and redeem the credit before the ledger catches up, or retain access through a cached permission after the role is removed. The inconsistency is not a race in the hardware sense; it is an architectural gap between copies. State transition: SOURCE_STATE_CHANGED -> REPLICA_NOT_YET_UPDATED -> DECISION_READS_STALE_COPY -> ACTION_ALLOWED -> DOUBLE_EFFECT. Variants include cache invalidation lag, search index staleness, event-driven projections, and read replicas. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1250 Exploitation Pattern: Acting on a Stale Copy of a Business Fact
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improper Preservation of Consistency Between Independent Representations of Shared State
attack_steps: Map every representation of the same business fact
Change the source of truth and immediately act on each replica
Measure the divergence window and what it permits
Confirm a double effect such as both refund and credit

text: Attack pattern: The attacker requests a restricted record and receives a 403, but the server has already loaded it, written an audit entry, incremented a counter, or queued an export. Comparing timing and error variants reveals the record's existence and sometimes its contents through a partial response or a downstream notification. State transition: REQUEST_RECEIVED -> ASSET_ACCESSED -> SIDE_EFFECT_OCCURRED -> AUTHORIZATION_CHECKED -> RESPONSE_DENIED. Variants include load-then-check controllers, export jobs, notification triggers, and counters incremented before denial. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1280 Exploitation Pattern: Denials That Arrive After the Asset Was Read
metadata.vulnerability_class: Access Control Check Implemented After Asset is Accessed
attack_steps: Identify endpoints that load or act on an object before checking access
Compare response timing and error variants for existing and non-existing objects
Look for side effects such as notifications or counters after a denial
Confirm disclosure or an irreversible effect

text: Attack pattern: The victim visits an attacker page that opens a socket to the application. The browser attaches the session cookie, the server completes the handshake without checking Origin, and the attacker page sends messages such as a profile change or an order action. The response may even be readable, turning the socket into a cross-origin data channel. State transition: MALICIOUS_PAGE_LOADED -> SOCKET_UPGRADE_SENT -> ORIGIN_NOT_VALIDATED -> COOKIE_AUTHENTICATED -> MESSAGES_EXCHANGED. Variants include socket-based chat, live order updates, notification streams, and admin consoles. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1385 Exploitation Pattern: Cross-Origin Sockets Acting with the Victim's Session
attack_steps: Discover WebSocket endpoints and the messages they accept
Open a socket from a different origin with the victim's cookies
Send a state-changing message and observe the effect
Read the response stream if the protocol permits it

text: Attack pattern: The attacker submits a price or quantity as 0x10 or 010. The validator reads it as ten or rejects it, while the pricing service reads it as sixteen or eight. The order is accepted at a value the attacker chose but the limit check evaluated a different number, producing an unintended charge or quota overrun. State transition: NUMERIC_INPUT_SENT -> VALIDATOR_PARSES_ONE_BASE -> BUSINESS_LOGIC_PARSES_ANOTHER -> VALUE_DIFFERS -> LIMIT_OR_PRICE_BYPASSED. Variants include hexadecimal, octal, leading zeros, scientific notation, and locale-specific separators. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1389 Exploitation Pattern: Hex, Octal, and Exponent Forms That Change the Number
metadata.vulnerability_class: Incorrect Parsing of Numbers with Different Radices
attack_steps: Identify numeric fields that affect price, quantity, or limits
Submit the same value in decimal, hex, octal, and exponent forms
Compare the validated value with the persisted value
Confirm the price or quota effect

text: Attack pattern: The attacker identifies the component from its banner or error page and tries the documented default. The credential works, giving access to configuration, data, or an integration that can move money or change entitlements. The same default works on other instances of the product. State transition: COMPONENT_IDENTIFIED -> DEFAULT_PAIR_TRIED -> PASSWORD_CHANGE_NOT_REQUIRED -> AUTHENTICATED -> BUSINESS_SYSTEM_CONTROLLED. Variants include admin consoles, broker dashboards, database users, and partner API accounts. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1392 Exploitation Pattern: Shipped Credentials Still Valid in Production
attack_steps: Identify reachable components and their default account conventions
Try documented defaults with rate-limited, authorized testing
Check whether a credential change is forced on first login
Confirm the business capability the account exposes

text: Attack pattern: The attacker obtains a session cookie from a shared machine, a backup, or a proxy log. Days or weeks later the cookie still works because the server never enforced an absolute or idle timeout. The attacker reads messages, changes payout details, or approves transactions as the victim. State transition: SESSION_CREATED -> TIMEOUT_NOT_ENFORCED -> COOKIE_RETAINED -> LONG_DELAY -> SESSION_STILL_VALID. Variants include remember-me cookies, mobile refresh tokens, API sessions, and impersonation links. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1463 Exploitation Pattern: Sessions That Never Expire on Shared Devices
attack_steps: Authenticate and record every session artifact and its stated lifetime
Wait beyond the idle and absolute thresholds
Reuse the artifact and observe acceptance
Confirm access to a sensitive action after the timeout

text: Attack pattern: The victim logs out or an administrator disables the account after a suspected compromise. The attacker, holding a copy of the cookie, continues to use the session. The interface shows the user as logged out, but the backend still accepts the artifact, so the attacker keeps access through the incident response. State transition: SESSION_ACTIVE -> LOGOUT_OR_REVOCATION -> SERVER_STATE_NOT_CLEARED -> OLD_ARTIFACT_REUSED -> ACCESS_CONTINUES. Variants include logout without server invalidation, password change without session rotation, and disabled accounts with live tokens. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1464 Exploitation Pattern: Sessions That Survive Logout and Revocation
attack_steps: Capture the session artifact before logout or revocation
Perform the termination action
Replay the artifact from an independent client
Confirm access to a sensitive action after termination

text: Attack pattern: The victim discovers suspicious activity and changes the password. The attacker's existing session, obtained with the old password, continues to work. The victim believes the account is secured, while the attacker still reads mail, changes settings, or approves payments from the retained session. State transition: OLD_CREDENTIAL_COMPROMISED -> SESSION_ACTIVE -> PASSWORD_CHANGED -> OTHER_SESSIONS_NOT_REVOKED -> ATTACKER_ACCESS_CONTINUES. Variants include password change, username change, MFA reset, and recovery-email change. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1466 Exploitation Pattern: Attacker Session Surviving the Victim's Password Change
metadata.vulnerability_class: Improper Session Invalidation after Authentication Credential Change
attack_steps: Establish two sessions with the same account
Change the password or username in one session
Replay the other session's artifact
Confirm sensitive access from the pre-change session

text: Attack pattern: The attacker captures the shared token from a less protected client, such as a browser extension or a mobile backup, and uses it against the web application. Because every client uses the same artifact, the server cannot distinguish the attacker's use from the legitimate device, and revoking the compromised device does not stop the attacker. State transition: SINGLE_ARTIFACT_ISSUED -> MULTIPLE_CLIENTS_USE_IT -> ORIGIN_NOT_BOUND -> ARTIFACT_CAPTURED -> REPLAY_ON_ANOTHER_CLIENT. Variants include shared API tokens, deterministic session IDs, and refresh tokens reused across devices. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1467 Exploitation Pattern: One Token Shared by Web, Mobile, and Integrations
metadata.vulnerability_class: Use of Singular Authentication Artifact for Multiple User Sessions
attack_steps: Authenticate on two clients and compare the artifacts
Capture the artifact from one client and use it on the other
Revoke one session and test the remaining client
Confirm access from the unintended client

text: Attack pattern: The attacker registers or updates an account with the victim's email or phone number and skips the confirmation step. The system now associates the victim's identifier with the attacker's account, so password recovery, invitations, or partner entitlements intended for the victim are delivered to the attacker. State transition: IDENTIFIER_SUBMITTED -> VERIFICATION_SKIPPED -> LINK_PERSISTED -> VICTIM_IDENTIFIER_ASSOCIATED -> RECOVERY_OR_INVITE_DIVERTED. Variants include unverified email registration, phone recovery without OTP, social linking by attribute match, and domain-claim without DNS proof. The attacker iterates until the business outcome, not merely an error message or response code, changes. Repeating the sequence across accounts or tenants turns a single-unit discrepancy into a systematic loss.

metadata.title: CWE-1470 Exploitation Pattern: Linking Accounts to Identifiers the Applicant Does Not Control
attack_steps: Submit an external identifier the tester does not control
Skip or replay the verification step
Check whether the link is persisted and treated as verified
Trigger recovery or invitation and observe where it is delivered

text: Attack pattern: borrow the identifier, keep the benefit. The attacker saves a build from a free account, intercepts the POST to the build-save endpoint, and replaces the background field with the identifier of a premium background observed on another profile. The response confirms the save and the build renders with the premium asset. State transition: BUILD_SAVED -> BACKGROUND_SUBSTITUTED -> ENTITLEMENT_NOT_CHECKED -> COSMETIC_PERSISTED -> PREMIUM_RENDERED. Variants include copying the identifier from a shared build link and reusing a premium asset after the subscription lapses.

metadata.title: Saving a Build With a Premium Background from a Free Account
metadata.report_title: Bypass restrict of member subscription to use custom background in https://3d.cs.money without prime subscription
attack_steps: Save a build with a free background and capture the request
Replace the background identifier with a premium one
Replay the request and reload the build
Confirm the premium cosmetic renders for the free account

text: Attack pattern: call the private operation without credentials. The attacker reads the public API documentation, selects a user operation, and sends the request with no signature or token. Most operations return an invalid request error, but the withdrawal-fee operation returns real fee data. State transition: DOCUMENTATION_READ -> PRIVATE_ENDPOINT_SELECTED -> UNSIGNED_REQUEST_SENT -> AUTH_FILTER_MISSING -> FINANCIAL_DATA_RETURNED. Variants include optional authentication that is skipped when the header is absent and routes that accept a stale token.

metadata.title: Calling a Documented User Operation Without a Session
metadata.report_title: POST /api/bitcoinWithdrawalFees returns financial data without authentication despite being documented as a USER OPERATION (private endpoint)
attack_steps: Collect the documented user operations from the API reference
Send each operation without a token or signature
Compare responses to identify the route that does not reject
Confirm the returned data is live private financial data

text: Attack pattern: send the value the slider cannot produce. The attacker opens the preferences page, captures the UpdateInvitationPreferencesMutation request, and replaces the threshold with a value above the displayed maximum. The mutation returns success and the preference is persisted. State transition: PREFERENCES_OPENED -> MUTATION_CAPTURED -> THRESHOLD_ABOVE_CEILING_SENT -> RANGE_NOT_VALIDATED -> PREFERENCE_PERSISTED. Variants include negative thresholds, values above the payout ceiling, and alternate mutations that write the same field.

metadata.title: Setting a Minimum Bounty Above the Slider Ceiling with a Crafted Mutation
metadata.report_title: Hacker can bypass minimum bounty amount restrictions in "invitation preferences" setting via UpdateInvitationPreferencesMutation GraphQL operation
attack_steps: Capture the preference mutation and note the legitimate range
Submit a value above the maximum and one below the minimum
Reload the preferences and confirm the stored value
Observe the effect on invitation filtering

text: Attack pattern: revive a dead invitation. The attacker, holding a limited staff role, opens the customer list and requests the invitation link for a customer who has already activated. The interface normally hides the action, but the retrieval endpoint still responds with a usable link. The attacker opens it and sets a new password. State transition: CUSTOMER_ACTIVATED -> RETRIEVAL_REQUESTED -> ACTIVATION_NOT_CHECKED -> LINK_RETURNED -> PASSWORD_RESET -> TAKEOVER. Variants include re-inviting the same address and replaying a previously captured link.

metadata.title: Reissuing an Invitation Link to Take Over an Activated Wholesale Account
metadata.report_title: Staff who only have apps and channels permission can do a takeover account at the wholesale store (Bypass get invitation link)
metadata.state_transition: CUSTOMER_ACTIVATED -> RETRIEVAL_REQUESTED -> ACTIVATION_NOT_CHECKED -> LINK_RETURNED -> PASSWORD_RESET -> TAKEOVER
attack_steps: Identify the invitation-link retrieval action and the roles that can reach it
Request the link for a customer who has already activated
Open the link and set a new password
Confirm access to the customer's wholesale account

text: Attack pattern: skip the gate and bind the device. The attacker uses a hijacked session to request an OTP device binding, bypasses the password prompt by calling the send and verify endpoints directly, and completes enrolment with a code delivered to their own phone. State transition: SESSION_HIJACKED -> ENROLMENT_STARTED -> PASSWORD_STEP_SKIPPED -> DEVICE_BOUND -> FUTURE_CODES_INTERCEPTED. Variants include adding a backup device and replacing an existing device without proving possession of the old one.

metadata.title: Enrolling an Attacker-Controlled OTP Device from a Hijacked Session
metadata.report_title: Bypassed password authentication before enabling OTP verification
attack_steps: Start two-factor enrolment and capture each request
Call the device-binding endpoints without the password step
Complete verification with a code sent to the attacker's phone
Log in again and confirm the attacker receives the OTP

text: Attack pattern: register, reset, log in, harvest. The attacker registers with an arbitrary address, requests a password reset for the pending account, sets a password, and logs in. The account is treated as active because the reset completed. The attacker then calls directory endpoints and pages through employee records. State transition: REGISTERED -> PENDING -> RESET_COMPLETED -> ACTIVE -> PROTECTED_ACCESS -> BULK_PII_READ. Variants include reusing the reset token and registering with an address the attacker does not control.

metadata.title: Registration, Reset, and Login Chain Exposing Employee Records
metadata.report_title: Unauthenticated Account Registration + Email Verification Bypass + PII Data Leak (2,480 Records) on portal
metadata.state_transition: REGISTERED -> PENDING -> RESET_COMPLETED -> ACTIVE -> PROTECTED_ACCESS -> BULK_PII_READ
attack_steps: Register an account with an address the attacker controls but does not verify
Request and complete a password reset on the pending account
Log in and check whether verification is still required
Call protected directory endpoints and measure the exposed records

text: Attack pattern: get approved with one identity, operate as another. The attacker submits identity fields for a controlled or synthetic person, uploads documents belonging to someone else, and is approved because the documents are valid in isolation. They then call the personal-information endpoint to replace name, birth date, and address after approval. State transition: APPLICATION_SUBMITTED -> DOCUMENTS_UPLOADED -> CROSS_FIELD_CHECK_SKIPPED -> VERIFIED -> PROFILE_MUTATED -> DIFFERENT_IDENTITY_OPERATES. Variants include changing the address only and re-verifying with a second person's document.

metadata.title: Verifying with One Identity and Transacting Under Another
metadata.report_title: Verification process done using different documents without corresponding to user information / User information can be changed after verification
metadata.state_transition: APPLICATION_SUBMITTED -> DOCUMENTS_UPLOADED -> CROSS_FIELD_CHECK_SKIPPED -> VERIFIED -> PROFILE_MUTATED -> DIFFERENT_IDENTITY_OPERATES
attack_steps: Submit identity fields and documents that do not match
Confirm approval despite the mismatch
Call the profile-write endpoint after approval
Verify that transactions use the new identity while KYC remains approved

text: Attack pattern: change whose account the OTP flow acts on. The attacker logs in to their own account, captures the OTP logout request, and replaces their user_id with the victim's. The server invalidates or reissues state for the victim, and the attacker completes the OTP login for that identifier, receiving a session as the victim. State transition: ATTACKER_LOGGED_IN -> USER_ID_SUBSTITUTED -> OTP_STATE_FOR_VICTIM -> CODE_VERIFIED -> VICTIM_SESSION_ISSUED. Variants include substituting the identifier only in the login call.

metadata.title: Logging In as the Victim by Substituting user_id in the OTP Flow
metadata.report_title: Improper Authentication - any user can login as other user with otp/logout & otp/login
attack_steps: Log in to an attacker-controlled account and capture the OTP logout and login requests
Replace user_id with the victim's identifier
Complete the OTP challenge for the substituted identifier
Confirm the resulting session belongs to the victim

text: Attack pattern: race the balance, then refund it. The attacker fires ten parallel invitation requests when only one invite remains. All ten read the same balance and all ten are accepted. The attacker then cancels the invitations, the balance is credited back, and the cycle repeats. State transition: QUOTA_READ -> PARALLEL_REQUESTS -> STALE_BALANCE_USED -> MULTIPLE_INVITES_SENT -> CANCEL_CREDITS_BACK -> QUOTA_OVERRUN. Variants include two-request races and cancellation of only some invitations.

metadata.title: Spending One Invite Many Times with Parallel Requests and Cancellations
metadata.report_title: Race condition in endpoint POST fetlife.com/users/invitation, allow attacker to generate unlimited invites
metadata.state_transition: QUOTA_READ -> PARALLEL_REQUESTS -> STALE_BALANCE_USED -> MULTIPLE_INVITES_SENT -> CANCEL_CREDITS_BACK -> QUOTA_OVERRUN
attack_steps: Reduce the account to a single remaining invitation
Send many invitation requests in parallel
Count the accepted invitations and the resulting balance
Cancel the invitations and confirm the balance is credited

text: Attack pattern: spend the whole keyspace. The attacker logs in with stolen credentials, reaches the activation step, and sends requests for every four-digit value. The endpoint answers uniformly and eventually accepts the correct code. State transition: CREDENTIALS_VALID -> OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED -> ATTEMPT_LIMIT_ABSENT -> KEYSPACE_ENUMERATED -> CODE_ACCEPTED -> SESSION_ACTIVATED. Variants include parallel guessing and retrying after the code rotates.

metadata.title: Enumerating the Entire OTP Space Against the Profile Activation Endpoint
metadata.report_title: Two-factor authentication bypass on Grab Android App
metadata.state_transition: CREDENTIALS_VALID -> OTP_CHALLENGE_ISSUED -> ATTEMPT_LIMIT_ABSENT -> KEYSPACE_ENUMERATED -> CODE_ACCEPTED -> SESSION_ACTIVATED
attack_steps: Reach the OTP challenge with valid credentials
Measure the response for wrong and repeated codes
Enumerate the full code space at a controlled rate
Confirm the session is activated with the accepted code

text: Attack pattern: add the address, skip the proof. The attacker starts an email change, captures the confirmation request, and completes the flow without the token that would be delivered to the target mailbox. The address becomes verified, and the attacker opens the private invitation or recovery message addressed to it. State transition: ADDRESS_ADDED -> CONFIRMATION_BYPASSED -> VERIFIED_STATE_SET -> MESSAGES_ROUTED -> PRIVATE_INVITATION_READ. Variants include reusing a token from another address and verifying through the password-reset path.

metadata.title: Claiming an Unverified Address to Read Its Private Invitation
metadata.report_title: Email Verification Bypass And Get access to user's private invitation.
attack_steps: Add an address the tester does not control and capture the flow
Complete the flow without the delivered confirmation token
Check whether the address is marked verified
Trigger an invitation or recovery and observe delivery

text: Attack pattern: become a new client on every request. The attacker captures a login request, adds an X-Forwarded-For value, and rotates it across attempts. The gateway treats each value as a distinct client and never blocks. State transition: LOGIN_ATTEMPT -> HEADER_ADDED -> THROTTLE_KEY_CHANGED -> COUNTER_RESET -> UNLIMITED_ATTEMPTS. Variants include X-Real-IP, Forwarded, and multiple comma-separated addresses.

metadata.title: Rotating X-Forwarded-For to Bypass Login Throttling
metadata.report_title: Rate limit bypass on passport.acronis.work using X-Forwarded-For request header
attack_steps: Trigger the throttle with repeated attempts from one apparent client
Add and rotate X-Forwarded-For across attempts
Confirm the throttle no longer blocks
Measure the sustained attempt rate achieved

text: Attack pattern: bind first, verify never. The attacker starts recovery setup, enters the victim's phone number, and skips the OTP step by calling the save endpoint directly. The number is stored as the recovery channel. Later authentication and recovery events route through that channel, and the attacker can trigger or observe the resulting state. State transition: RECOVERY_SETUP -> PHONE_ENTERED -> OTP_SKIPPED -> CHANNEL_SAVED -> CODES_ROUTED -> RECOVERY_INFLUENCED. Variants include changing an existing number and adding a backup channel.

metadata.title: Adding a Victim Phone Number and Receiving Their 2FA Codes
metadata.report_title: Bypassing the victim's phone number OTP in the account recovery process on HackerOne
metadata.state_transition: RECOVERY_SETUP -> PHONE_ENTERED -> OTP_SKIPPED -> CHANNEL_SAVED -> CODES_ROUTED -> RECOVERY_INFLUENCED
attack_steps: Start recovery setup and enter a phone number the tester does not control
Call the save endpoint without completing the OTP step
Confirm the number is stored as a trusted recovery channel
Trigger an authentication or recovery event and observe routing

text: Attack pattern: prove the factor you are installing. The attacker, holding the password, generates a TOTP secret locally, calls the update mutation with a code from that new secret, and the server accepts it. The account now uses the attacker's authenticator and the victim's codes stop working. State transition: PASSWORD_KNOWN -> NEW_SECRET_GENERATED -> UPDATE_MUTATION_SENT -> NEW_CODE_ACCEPTED -> FACTOR_REPLACED -> VICTIM_LOCKED_OUT. Variants include regenerating backup codes and removing the old device.

metadata.title: Re-Enrolling the Authenticator with a Known Setup Key
metadata.report_title: Changing the 2FA secret key and backup codes without knowing the 2FA OTP
metadata.state_transition: PASSWORD_KNOWN -> NEW_SECRET_GENERATED -> UPDATE_MUTATION_SENT -> NEW_CODE_ACCEPTED -> FACTOR_REPLACED -> VICTIM_LOCKED_OUT
attack_steps: Authenticate with the password and reach the 2FA settings
Generate a new TOTP secret and capture the update request
Submit a code from the new secret without an old-factor code
Confirm the new factor works and the old one does not

text: Attack pattern: use the identifier as the credential. The attacker obtains or guesses a payment UUID from a link, an export, or a referrer, opens the edit URL while logged out, and submits new billing details. The record is updated because the handler trusts the identifier and never checks who is calling. State transition: PAYMENT_ID_OBTAINED -> EDIT_PAGE_OPENED -> OWNERSHIP_NOT_CHECKED -> FORM_SUBMITTED -> BILLING_DATA_REWRITTEN. Variants include sequential identifiers and bulk edit endpoints.

metadata.title: Editing a Payment Record by Opening Its Identifier While Logged Out
metadata.report_title: Unauthenticated IDOR allows modification of payment customer billing information
attack_steps: Obtain a payment identifier from a link, export, or referrer
Open the edit page in a logged-out browser
Submit modified billing information
Read the record back to confirm the change

text: Attack pattern: leave, get invited, repeat. The researcher joins a program, uses the leave flow to trigger an automated invitation, accepts it, and repeats. The security@ forwarding path supplies additional invitations from inbound mail. State transition: PROGRAM_JOINED -> LEAVE_REQUESTED -> REWARD_INVITE_ISSUED -> INVITE_ACCEPTED -> CYCLE_REPEATED -> INVITES_HARVESTED. Variants include forwarding multiple addresses and chaining the reward with other automated invitation sources.

metadata.title: Cycling Leave and Rejoin to Collect Automated Private Invites
metadata.report_title: Harvesting all private invites using leave program fast-tracked invitation and security email forwarding feature
metadata.state_transition: PROGRAM_JOINED -> LEAVE_REQUESTED -> REWARD_INVITE_ISSUED -> INVITE_ACCEPTED -> CYCLE_REPEATED -> INVITES_HARVESTED
attack_steps: Join a private program and record the invitation state
Use the leave flow and observe the reward invitation
Accept and repeat the cycle
Count distinct private invitations obtained by one account

text: Attack pattern: read the secret from the app, then satisfy the check with it. The attacker with a hijacked session requests a diagnostic or error-producing endpoint, extracts the value the 2FA flow compares against, and submits it. They then change the recovery email or disable 2FA to persist. State transition: SESSION_HIJACKED -> DEBUG_VALUE_DISCLOSED -> 2FA_CHECK_SATISFIED -> SENSITIVE_SETTING_CHANGED -> ACCESS_PERSISTED. Variants include verbose error bodies and client-side feature flags.

metadata.title: Using a Leaked Debug Value to Skip 2FA and Persist Access
metadata.report_title: Information disclosure -> 2fa bypass -> POST exploitation
attack_steps: Reach the 2FA step and capture the requests and responses
Probe debug, error, and diagnostic surfaces for accepted values
Submit the disclosed value to complete the check
Perform a post-compromise action and confirm persistence

text: Attack pattern: tell the browser the code was right. The attacker submits login credentials, receives the 2FA prompt, submits a wrong code, and intercepts the response. They change the failure flag to success and forward it. The client navigates to the authenticated area and the server accepts the session. State transition: CREDENTIALS_ACCEPTED -> 2FA_PROMPTED -> WRONG_CODE_REJECTED -> RESPONSE_MODIFIED -> AUTHENTICATED_AREA_REACHED. Variants include changing a status code and editing a JSON boolean.

metadata.title: Editing the Verification Response to Reach the Authenticated Area
metadata.report_title: 2FA Bypass via Response Manipulation on Login Page
attack_steps: Log in with valid credentials and reach the 2FA prompt
Submit a wrong code and intercept the response
Modify the success flag or status and forward it
Access a protected page that requires completed 2FA

text: Attack pattern: reopen the receipt. The attacker completes a purchase, captures the checkout router URL, and observes how the identifier is formed. They modify the key and brute-force neighbouring values, receiving confirmation pages for other orders. State transition: CHECKOUT_COMPLETED -> ROUTER_URL_CAPTURED -> KEY_MODIFIED -> OWNERSHIP_NOT_CHECKED -> FOREIGN_PAYMENT_PAGE_RENDERED. Variants include changing only the numeric suffix and reusing a key after logout.

metadata.title: Enumerating Checkout Identifiers to Read Other Buyers' Payment Pages
metadata.report_title: Bypassing one-time checkout router page (revealing payment information)
attack_steps: Complete a purchase and capture the confirmation URL
Analyse how the checkout key is constructed
Enumerate neighbouring keys and record successful pages
Confirm the displayed data belongs to other buyers

text: Attack pattern: borrow trust, then change who you are. The attacker registers, completes OTP, and selects trust this device. They then change the account email to the victim's unregistered address. The trusted-device marker remains, so future logins skip OTP and the session is treated as the victim. State transition: OTP_VERIFIED -> DEVICE_TRUSTED -> EMAIL_CHANGED_TO_VICTIM -> TRUST_NOT_REVOKED -> OTP_SKIPPED -> IMPERSONATION. Variants include changing the phone number and adding a second trusted device.

metadata.title: Changing the Email to an Unregistered Victim and Keeping the Trusted Session
metadata.report_title: 2FA Bypass leads to impersonation of legitimate users
metadata.state_transition: OTP_VERIFIED -> DEVICE_TRUSTED -> EMAIL_CHANGED_TO_VICTIM -> TRUST_NOT_REVOKED -> OTP_SKIPPED -> IMPERSONATION
attack_steps: Register an account, complete OTP, and trust the device
Change the email to the victim's unregistered address
Log out and log back in
Confirm no OTP is requested and the account is treated as the victim

text: Attack pattern: approve yourself. The attacker creates a vacancy, captures the final status mutation, and changes the requested status from pending or draft to published. The resolver trusts the supplied value and the vacancy appears publicly without any review event. State transition: VACANCY_CREATED -> STATUS_MUTATION_CAPTURED -> PUBLISHED_STATUS_SUPPLIED -> APPROVAL_NOT_CHECKED -> VACANCY_LIVE. Variants include editing an already approved vacancy to add new content.

metadata.title: Calling UpdateVacancyStatus to Publish an Unreviewed Vacancy
metadata.report_title: inDriver Job - Admin Approval Bypass
attack_steps: Create a vacancy and capture the status mutation
Submit a published or approved status directly
Check whether the vacancy is publicly visible
Confirm no approval event exists in the audit trail

text: Attack pattern: earn on credit, spend immediately. The attacker places a large cash-on-delivery order, receives points as soon as the status becomes processing, and spends them on a second order. They then refuse delivery or cancel, and the points are never reversed. State transition: ORDER_PLACED -> STATUS_PROCESSING -> POINTS_CREDITED -> POINTS_SPENT -> ORDER_CANCELLED -> NO_REVERSAL. Variants include partial refunds and failed deliveries.

metadata.title: Earning and Spending Points on Orders That Are Never Paid
metadata.report_title: Gaining unlimited bonus points on websites with WooCommerce Points and Rewards
metadata.state_transition: ORDER_PLACED -> STATUS_PROCESSING -> POINTS_CREDITED -> POINTS_SPENT -> ORDER_CANCELLED -> NO_REVERSAL
attack_steps: Place an order using a payment method that reaches processing before settlement
Confirm points are credited and spendable
Spend the points on a second order
Cancel or refuse the first order and check for reversal

text: Attack pattern: type the URL the menu hides. The attacker signs in with a member role, navigates directly to the billing payment route, and the page renders with the organization's payment methods. They can start adding a card or view billing details despite lacking the billing role. State transition: MEMBER_SESSION -> BILLING_URL_ENTERED -> ROLE_NOT_CHECKED -> PAYMENT_PAGE_RENDERED -> FINANCIAL_ACTION_AVAILABLE. Variants include calling the underlying billing APIs directly.

metadata.title: Navigating Directly to the Billing URL with Member Privileges
metadata.report_title: A member-member privilege could access the billing payment page even though the billing page is hidden from the menu
attack_steps: Sign in with a member-only role
Navigate directly to the billing payment route
Confirm the page renders with organization payment data
Attempt a billing action and observe whether it is accepted

text: Attack pattern: slow down just enough. The attacker sends subscription requests with a fixed delay that stays under the burst threshold. The 429 disappears and every request is accepted, allowing a large list of addresses to be subscribed. State transition: REQUEST_SENT -> BURST_LIMIT_HIT -> PACE_REDUCED -> THROTTLE_EVADED -> BULK_SUBSCRIPTION. Variants include distributing requests across source addresses and using case variants of the same address.

metadata.title: Sending Bulk Subscription Requests Through a Fixed Throttle
metadata.report_title: No rate limit in email subscription
attack_steps: Send a burst and observe the 429 behaviour
Reduce the request rate until the 429 stops
Sustain the rate with a list of target addresses
Confirm all requests are accepted

text: Attack pattern: guess six digits, own the factor. The attacker starts 2FA setup on a hijacked session, requests the email code, and brute-forces it with a high-volume request set. The code is accepted, the email is marked verified, and the attacker binds their phone. State transition: SETUP_STARTED -> CODE_REQUESTED -> ATTEMPT_LIMIT_ABSENT -> CODE_GUESSED -> EMAIL_VERIFIED -> ATTACKER_PHONE_BOUND. Variants include parallel guessing and requesting a fresh code without invalidating the old one.

metadata.title: Guessing the Email Code to Bind an Attacker Phone
metadata.report_title: Email Verification Bypass by bruteforcing when setting up 2FA
metadata.state_transition: SETUP_STARTED -> CODE_REQUESTED -> ATTEMPT_LIMIT_ABSENT -> CODE_GUESSED -> EMAIL_VERIFIED -> ATTACKER_PHONE_BOUND
attack_steps: Start 2FA setup and request the email confirmation code
Submit wrong codes and observe the attempt limit
Enumerate the six-digit space or a plausible subset
Bind an attacker phone after the email is verified

text: Attack pattern: link first, authenticate later. The attacker obtains the victim's user ID, calls the linking endpoint with it, and receives a challenge for the attacker's device. They submit a valid code to the verify endpoint, which accepts it without the victim's password, and then log in using the linked factor alone. State transition: VICTIM_ID_KNOWN -> LINK_REQUESTED -> ID_NOT_BOUND_TO_SESSION -> DEVICE_BOUND -> CODE_VERIFIED -> LOGIN_WITHOUT_PASSWORD. Variants include linking to accounts that already have a factor and reusing a stale challenge.

metadata.title: Linking an Attacker Device to a Victim Who Never Enabled 2FA
metadata.report_title: Account takeover w/o interaction for a user that doesn't have 2fa enabled via 2fa linking and improper auth at /api/2fa/verify
metadata.state_transition: VICTIM_ID_KNOWN -> LINK_REQUESTED -> ID_NOT_BOUND_TO_SESSION -> DEVICE_BOUND -> CODE_VERIFIED -> LOGIN_WITHOUT_PASSWORD
attack_steps: Obtain a victim user ID from a profile, API response, or invite
Call the linking endpoint with that ID
Complete verification with the attacker's device
Log in using the linked factor without the password

text: Attack pattern: narrow the space, then sweep it. The attacker submits the password, captures the MFA request, and sends a numeric range of candidate codes. Most responses redirect to the prompt, but one returns the authenticated redirect. State transition: PASSWORD_ACCEPTED -> MFA_PROMPTED -> CODE_RANGE_SENT -> ATTEMPT_LIMIT_ABSENT -> CODE_ACCEPTED -> LOGIN_COMPLETED. Variants include parallel sweeps and repeated challenges after the code rotates.

metadata.title: Enumerating a Narrow Code Range to Complete Login
metadata.report_title: 2FA bypass possible on https://authsvc.singlestore.com
metadata.state_transition: PASSWORD_ACCEPTED -> MFA_PROMPTED -> CODE_RANGE_SENT -> ATTEMPT_LIMIT_ABSENT -> CODE_ACCEPTED -> LOGIN_COMPLETED
attack_steps: Authenticate with the victim's email and password
Capture the MFA verification request
Send a numeric range of candidate codes
Identify the success redirect and load the authenticated area

text: Attack pattern: guess tokens until one applies. The attacker sends many parallel requests with random bearer tokens and a known promo code. The endpoint answers quickly and one token is accepted, letting the attacker apply promotions or infer account state. State transition: PROMO_ENDPOINT_FOUND -> RANDOM_TOKENS_SENT -> NO_THROTTLE -> VALID_TOKEN_FOUND -> PROMOTION_APPLIED. Variants include reusing a discovered token across promotions.

metadata.title: Brute-Forcing Bearer Tokens Against the Promotion Endpoint
metadata.report_title: The Uber Promo Customer Endpoint Does Not Implement Multifactor Authentication, Blacklisting or Rate Limiting
attack_steps: Identify the promotion endpoint and the token format
Send parallel requests with random tokens and a known promo
Look for a response that confirms a valid token
Apply the promotion and confirm the account effect

text: Attack pattern: use the door without the lock. The attacker removes 2FA and confirms the main form blocks submission, then opens the program's embedded form and submits successfully. A blacklisted reporter can use the same path. State transition: REQUIREMENT_ACTIVE -> MAIN_FORM_BLOCKED -> EMBEDDED_FORM_USED -> POLICY_NOT_CHECKED -> REPORT_CREATED. Variants include API submission and mobile clients.

metadata.title: Submitting Through the Embedded Form Without 2FA or Clearing the Blacklist
metadata.report_title: Hacker can bypass 2FA requirement and reporter blacklist through embedded submission form
attack_steps: Identify a program requirement and confirm it blocks the main form
Open the embedded submission form for the same program
Submit a report and observe acceptance
Repeat with a blacklisted account if one is available

text: Attack pattern: verify one address, provision another. The attacker starts signup with an address they control, captures the provisioning request, and replaces EmailAddress with the victim's address. The service creates or activates the account for the victim while the verification state belongs to the attacker's session. State transition: SIGNUP_STARTED -> PROVISION_REQUEST_CAPTURED -> EMAIL_PARAMETER_SUBSTITUTED -> IDENTITY_MISMATCH_NOT_CHECKED -> VICTIM_ACCOUNT_PROVISIONED. Variants include case variants and adding a second address field.

metadata.title: Changing EmailAddress During Signup to Activate an Existing Account
metadata.report_title: Email verification bypass via request to endpoint accounts.insightly.com/signup/provisionuser
attack_steps: Start signup with a controlled address and capture the provisioning request
Replace EmailAddress with the victim's address
Complete the flow and observe account creation
Attempt login or password recovery for the victim address

text: Attack pattern: free one slot, then race it. The attacker fills the space to ten folders, deletes one, and immediately fires a burst of creation requests. Multiple requests pass the count check and the space ends up with more folders than the plan allows. State transition: LIMIT_REACHED -> FOLDER_DELETED -> COUNT_READ_AS_NINE -> PARALLEL_CREATES -> QUOTA_EXCEEDED. Variants include repeated cycles and concurrent deletes mixed with creates.

metadata.title: Deleting One Folder and Racing Creation to Exceed the Ten-Folder Limit
metadata.report_title: Race Condition in Folder Creation Allows Bypassing Folder Limit
attack_steps: Create folders until the limit is reached
Delete one folder to free a slot
Send many folder-creation requests simultaneously
Count the resulting folders and confirm the limit is exceeded

text: Attack pattern: accept after the door closes. Admin A invites B with admin rights. A is then removed from the team, but B's invitation remains valid and B accepts it, obtaining admin access despite the removal. State transition: ADMIN_A_INVITES_B -> A_REMOVED -> INVITE_NOT_REVOKED -> B_ACCEPTS -> ADMIN_ACCESS_GRANTED. Variants include B already having accepted and retaining membership.

metadata.title: Accepting an Invite Issued by a Removed Admin to Regain Access
metadata.report_title: Pending invites remain valid even after the inviter is removed.
attack_steps: Invite a second user with admin privileges
Remove the inviter from the team
Accept the pending invitation as the second user
Confirm admin access persists

text: Attack pattern: subtract a line item. The attacker selects two articles, captures the bulk purchase request, and adds or sets a quantity to a negative number. The total drops below the price of the items actually requested, and the order is accepted. State transition: ITEMS_SELECTED -> BULK_REQUEST_CAPTURED -> NEGATIVE_QUANTITY_INJECTED -> TOTAL_REDUCED -> ORDER_ACCEPTED. Variants include fractional negatives and large negative values that flip the total sign.

metadata.title: Adding a Negative Quantity Alongside a Real Item to Lower the Price
metadata.report_title: An attacker can buy marketplace articles for lower prices as it allows for negative quantity values
attack_steps: Add two or more items and capture the bulk purchase request
Insert a negative quantity for one line item
Submit and compare the charged total with the catalogue sum
Confirm the positive items are still fulfilled

text: Attack pattern: accept an invitation the rules exclude. A researcher outside the permitted jurisdiction receives an automated private invite, accepts it, and can submit reports to a program that is legally restricted. State transition: PROGRAM_RESTRICTED -> INVITE_GENERATED -> JURISDICTION_NOT_CHECKED -> INVITE_ACCEPTED -> INELIGIBLE_PARTICIPATION. Variants include residence changes after invitation and proxy-based eligibility claims.

metadata.title: Accepting an Invitation for a Program Restricted to Another Country
metadata.report_title: Proper verification is not done before sending invitations to researchers for certain private programs with rules e.g. Participants must be US-based
attack_steps: Identify a private program with a jurisdiction restriction
Receive or obtain an automated invitation
Accept it and attempt to submit a report
Confirm participation despite the stated restriction

text: Attack pattern: change one character the mail system ignores. The attacker enters an address at a denied domain but replaces the i with İ. The denylist comparison fails to match, the invitation is sent, and the mail system normalizes the address back to the denied domain. State transition: DENIED_DOMAIN_CONFIGURED -> ADDRESS_WITH_UNICODE_SUBMITTED -> RAW_COMPARISON_MISSES -> INVITATION_SENT -> BLOCKED_DOMAIN_REACHED. Variants include other homoglyphs, trailing dots, and case variants.

metadata.title: Inviting a Blocked Domain by Substituting the Letter I
metadata.report_title: Bypassing the block of Security Domain Restriction and normally invite blocked domains with special characters
attack_steps: Configure a denied domain in the tenant policy
Submit an address at that domain using a Unicode equivalent character
Observe that the invitation is accepted and sent
Confirm delivery or acceptance at the denied domain

text: Attack pattern: decrement the filename. The attacker sends a chat message, opens the transcript, and notices the URL ends in an incrementing number. They request 1.txt and read an earlier conversation that contains a user's password, then log in as that user. State transition: TRANSCRIPT_OPENED -> FILENAME_ENUMERATED -> OWNERSHIP_NOT_CHECKED -> FOREIGN_TRANSCRIPT_READ -> CREDENTIAL_RECOVERED. Variants include guessing adjacent numbers and reusing an old transcript URL after logout.

metadata.title: Reading Another User's Transcript to Recover a Password
metadata.lab_title: Insecure direct object references
attack_steps: Send a chat message and open the transcript
Observe the filename pattern and decrement or increment it
Read transcripts belonging to other users
Use any recovered credential to confirm takeover

text: Attack pattern: reuse the admin's verb. The attacker logs in as an administrator in one session, captures the promotion request, and replays it with a non-admin session. The server sees POST and performs the promotion. State transition: ADMIN_REQUEST_CAPTURED -> METHOD_IDENTIFIED_AS_GATE -> NON_ADMIN_SESSION_USED -> ROLE_NOT_CHECKED -> SELF_PROMOTED. Variants include changing GET to POST and adding method-override headers.

metadata.title: Replaying the Admin Promotion Request from a Non-Admin Session
metadata.lab_title: Method-based access control can be circumvented
attack_steps: Capture the admin promotion request and note the method and body
Replay it with a non-admin session
Change the username to the attacker's account
Confirm the new role and access the admin panel

text: Attack pattern: start at step two. The attacker captures the admin confirmation request, then replays it with their own session and username. The server processes the confirmation without checking the role because it assumes the first step already did. State transition: PROMOTION_INITIATED -> CONFIRMATION_CAPTURED -> NON_ADMIN_REPLAY -> STEP_AUTHORIZATION_MISSING -> ROLE_CHANGED. Variants include skipping intermediate steps and reordering the workflow.

metadata.title: Skipping to the Unprotected Confirmation Step to Promote an Account
metadata.lab_title: Multi-step process with no access control on one step
attack_steps: Capture every request in the admin role-change workflow
Replay the confirmation step with a non-admin session
Set the target to the attacker's username
Verify the role change and admin access

text: Attack pattern: claim to have come from the admin panel. The attacker captures the admin promotion request, notes the Referer value, and replays the request with a non-admin session plus the same Referer. The endpoint accepts it and changes the role. State transition: ADMIN_REQUEST_CAPTURED -> REFERER_OBSERVED -> NON_ADMIN_REQUEST_SENT -> REFERER_TRUSTED -> ROLE_CHANGED. Variants include removing the header, using a partial match, and adding an Origin header.

metadata.title: Adding an Admin Referer to a Non-Admin Promotion Request
metadata.lab_title: Referer-based access control
attack_steps: Capture the admin promotion request and its Referer
Replay it with a non-admin session
Set the Referer to the admin panel URL
Confirm the role change and admin access

text: Attack pattern: read the map, walk in. The attacker requests robots.txt, finds a Disallow entry for the admin panel, and opens that path directly. The panel renders without a login and the delete action works. State transition: ROBOTS_READ -> ADMIN_PATH_DISCOVERED -> DIRECT_REQUEST -> AUTHORIZATION_ABSENT -> USER_DELETED. text: Attack pattern: read the script, not the menu. The attacker views the page source, finds a conditional block that constructs the admin URL, and opens it directly. The edge sees a public path and forwards the request; the backend routes to the admin panel. The attacker triggers a reset for their own account, observes the internal lookup, then submits a username followed by an encoded ampersand and a candidate parameter. Error messages reveal which parameter names the internal API accepts. A fragment character truncates the remaining query so the injected value takes effect. text: Attack pattern: ask for someone else's challenge. The attacker logs in, receives the second-factor prompt, and changes verify to the victim's username before submitting. The attacker logs in with the victim's username and password, reaches the code prompt, and instead of submitting a code navigates to the account URL. text: Attack pattern: refresh and guess. The attacker authenticates with the victim's credentials, captures the code submission, and builds a macro that fetches a fresh login page before each attempt so the challenge stays valid. text: Attack pattern: my token, your account. The attacker requests a reset for their own account, opens the link, and intercepts the confirmation request. They replace the username with the victim's and submit a new password. The server validates the still-valid token and updates the victim's credential. The email is delivered by the real application but points at the attacker. The victim clicks, the token arrives in the attacker's logs, and the attacker completes the reset. text: Attack pattern: one request, many guesses. The attacker captures the login request, changes the password value from a string to an array of candidates, and sends it once. The server iterates the values and issues a session for the matching one. The attacker detects success by a redirect or by which password the account now expects. text: Attack pattern: launder failures with your own success. The attacker sends two victim attempts, then logs in with their own account to clear the counter, and repeats. The victim's candidate list is exhausted without ever triggering the block. text: Attack pattern: send the same logical value as a string, number, boolean, null, and array, then compare which representation passes the business check. Precondition: the attacker can reach a workflow whose decision depends on a typed comparison, such as a plan check, role check, or quantity check. The attacker drives the workflow through identify a request field that controls entitlement, role, quantity, or price; then capture the baseline request with the legitimate type and record the decision; then resend the request with string, numeric, boolean, null, and array variants of the same field; then compare the resulting server-side state with the state produced by the legitimate value. The transition succeeds because the comparison succeeds under the language's coercion rules even though the attacker never supplied the value the business rule required. State transition: unprivileged request -> coerced comparison -> policy branch taken as if the privileged value were present -> protected action allowed. Variants include string zero versus numeric zero, boolean true versus string true, null versus empty string, array wrapping of a scalar, and precision loss between JSON number and database integer. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: hold one factor constant while changing the principal, tenant, usage count, or time window that the rule also depends on. Precondition: the workflow exposes a decision that depends on more than one factor, such as owner plus object, plan plus feature, or coupon plus redemption count. The attacker drives the workflow through enumerate the factors named in the business rule for the target feature; then capture a legitimate request and note which factors the server actually evaluates; then vary each unevaluated factor while leaving the checked factor valid; then confirm the benefit in a second account, tenant, or billing period. The transition succeeds because the comparison examines only the factor the attacker controls and ignores the factor that would have denied the request. State transition: eligible-looking request -> partial comparison -> missing factor assumed valid -> benefit granted to an ineligible principal. Variants include object id checked without owner, coupon checked without redemption count, feature flag checked without plan, tenant id checked without membership, and time window checked without server clock. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: submit ambiguous input whose meaning changes between the edge parser, the framework, and the application code. Precondition: more than one component parses the request, or the application decodes input after a security decision. The attacker drives the workflow through identify a parameter that passes through a proxy, WAF, framework, and application parser; then introduce duplicate keys, mixed encodings, or delimiter characters; then compare the value observed by the filter with the value used by the business logic; then confirm the divergent interpretation changes an authorization or pricing outcome. The transition succeeds because each layer believes it evaluated the same value, but the value that reaches the business decision was normalised differently. State transition: ambiguous request -> filter sees benign value -> downstream parser sees privileged value -> protected action executes. Variants include duplicate query keys, semicolon delimiters, double URL encoding, Unicode normalisation, parameter pollution, and conflicting Content-Type bodies. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

metadata.title: Attack chain: CWE-115: Misinterpretation of Input

text: Attack pattern: place the dangerous characters or values behind an encoding or transformation that occurs after validation. Precondition: the application validates input and later decodes, normalises, or rewrites it before the sensitive operation. The attacker drives the workflow through locate a field that is validated and then transformed before use; then identify the transformation order in code or by differential probing; then encode the payload so the validator sees a safe form and the sink sees the dangerous form; then verify the sink effect rather than the validation response. The transition succeeds because the validator and the sink operate on different representations, so the check never sees the value that matters. State transition: raw input validated -> transformation changes meaning -> sink receives unvalidated value -> policy bypass. Variants include validation before URL decoding, before Unicode normalisation, before XML entity expansion, before template rendering, and before case folding. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

metadata.title: Attack chain: CWE-179: Incorrect Behavior Order: Early Validation

text: Attack pattern: append or prepend attacker-controlled characters to a value that already matches the checked fragment. Precondition: the application compares a security-relevant string with a prefix, suffix, or truncated form. The attacker drives the workflow through identify token, domain, coupon, or identifier checks in the workflow; then determine the compared slice by varying characters inside and outside it; then craft a value that matches the slice but differs elsewhere; then confirm the action succeeds with the forged value. The transition succeeds because the unchecked remainder is never compared, so a value that differs outside the compared slice passes. State transition: attacker value with valid fragment -> partial comparison -> remainder ignored -> authenticated or authorised action allowed. Variants include prefix matching of API keys, suffix matching of email domains, fixed-length token comparison, SQL LIKE without escaping, and database collation truncation. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: supply numeric input in a form that coerces to a smaller or truncated value at the persistence boundary. Precondition: the workflow accepts a numeric field that is later cast, truncated, or converted for storage or calculation. The attacker drives the workflow through identify numeric fields used in price, quantity, fee, or balance calculations; then submit decimals, scientific notation, leading signs, and values beyond the column range; then compare the displayed value with the persisted value and the charged total; then repeat at the boundary where the cast occurs. The transition succeeds because the cast changes the value without an error, so downstream checks operate on a number the attacker chose indirectly. State transition: crafted numeric input -> silent coercion -> truncated quantity or amount -> underpayment or over-credit persisted. Variants include float to integer truncation, string to integer prefix parsing, 64-bit to 32-bit narrowing, decimal scale truncation, and NaN or infinity handling. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: drive a counter or quantity past its type boundary and observe the wrapped value used by the business rule. Precondition: the workflow exposes an increment, decrement, or accumulation operation on a fixed-width numeric field. The attacker drives the workflow through identify counters, quantities, loyalty points, or balances with a fixed-width type; then approach the boundary with legitimate operations; then cross the boundary with one more increment or a negative conversion; then confirm the wrapped value in the persisted balance or order total. The transition succeeds because the arithmetic wraps silently and the resulting value satisfies a check that the true value would fail. State transition: near-boundary value -> increment or negative conversion -> wrap to extreme value -> policy check inverted -> benefit granted. Variants include unsigned underflow from a negative refund, 8-bit or 16-bit quantity wrap, 32-bit points overflow, and page offset wrap in pagination. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: force a downstream dependency to fail while the caller proceeds, then observe whether the business state is still committed. Precondition: the workflow calls a payment, inventory, authorization, or persistence function whose failure is recoverable. The attacker drives the workflow through identify calls whose success is a precondition for the business action; then induce failure through invalid input, dependency timeout, or quota exhaustion; then observe whether the workflow still advances; then reconcile the committed business record with the failed dependency. The transition succeeds because the caller never inspects the failure result, so the workflow advances with an unfulfilled precondition. State transition: request accepted -> dependency returns failure -> caller ignores status -> success state committed without the required side effect. Variants include ignored boolean return, ignored error code, ignored database row count, ignored payment gateway status, and ignored authorization decision. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: produce a return value that is truthy or non-null on failure so the incorrect check treats it as success. Precondition: the workflow consumes an API whose contract distinguishes success, failure, and empty results in a non-obvious way. The attacker drives the workflow through read the dependency contract for success, failure, empty, and partial results; then induce each non-success shape; then observe which shapes pass the caller's check; then confirm the business action completed despite the non-success result. The transition succeeds because the check tests a proxy for success rather than the documented success condition. State transition: dependency returns failure-shaped value -> incorrect check passes -> workflow commits -> inconsistent business state. Variants include null-versus-status confusion, zero-means-success inversion, empty-list treated as success, partial-success treated as complete, and error object truthiness. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: submit null, empty, zero, duplicate, maximum-length, and conflicting values to a workflow that assumes normal input. Precondition: the workflow has an implicit assumption about the presence or range of a value. The attacker drives the workflow through list the assumptions each workflow step makes about its inputs; then send the smallest violating value for each assumption; then observe the state transition and error handling; then check whether the outcome grants access or commits partial data. The transition succeeds because the missing boundary branch is handled by a default, a catch-all, or no code at all, and that default is permissive. State transition: unusual input -> missing boundary branch -> default or undefined state -> permissive outcome or partial commit. Variants include null quantity, zero price, empty role list, duplicate redemption, maximum-length identifier, and missing optional step. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: cause a failure in the middle of a multi-step operation and inspect the state left behind. Precondition: the workflow performs two or more dependent writes, calls, or state transitions. The attacker drives the workflow through map the ordered writes and external calls in the workflow; then force a failure after the first successful step; then inspect every store for partial state; then retry the workflow to see whether the partial state becomes an advantage. The transition succeeds because the handler suppresses the failure without undoing the steps that already succeeded. State transition: step one commits -> later step throws -> handler swallows -> partial state persists -> attacker repeats or upgrades. Variants include swallowed exception after payment capture, partial account creation, orphaned coupon redemption, half-applied role change, and missing compensating refund. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: trigger a condition the application detects, then verify whether the business action still completes. text: Attack pattern: drive the workflow into an unhandled type, null, or range error and inspect the response and the persisted state. text: Attack pattern: place traversal, encoding, or delimiter sequences in a permitted path so the authorization check approves the raw form. text: Attack pattern: capture or obtain the password hash and replay it in the authentication request. text: Attack pattern: force the privilege-drop operation to fail and observe whether the sensitive action still runs with elevated rights. Precondition: the application deliberately drops privileges before handling untrusted input or executing a subprocess. text: Attack pattern: place the attacker's valid CSRF token in a cross-site request aimed at the victim's session. Precondition: the application checks a CSRF token but does not associate it with the session or user. The attacker drives the workflow through capture a state-changing request and its CSRF token; then log in as a second user and swap in the first user's token; then confirm the request is accepted; then deliver the cross-site form with the attacker's token. The transition succeeds because the server accepts any token it issued, so the attacker can supply their own and still pass the check. State transition: attacker obtains token -> cross-site request includes it -> victim session sends cookie -> server accepts token -> state changed. Variants include global token pool, token validated only for format, token reused across accounts, and token not rotated at login. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: inject a known csrf cookie into the victim and submit a form whose token matches it. Precondition: the application uses the double-submit cookie pattern for CSRF protection. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm the body token must equal the csrf cookie; then find a cookie-injection primitive such as a CRLF in a search response; then set csrf=fake for the victim; then submit a cross-site form with csrf=fake. The transition succeeds because the attacker can choose both sides of the comparison, so equality proves nothing about the victim's intent. State transition: attacker picks token -> injects matching cookie -> cross-site form sends token -> server compares equal -> state changed. Variants include CRLF cookie injection, subdomain cookie tossing, cookie fixed by a related app, and double-submit without signing. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: inject the attacker's csrfKey into the victim and submit the matching token. Precondition: the application binds CSRF tokens to a cookie that is not the session cookie. The attacker drives the workflow through capture the csrfKey cookie and matching token; then find a cookie-injection primitive; then set csrfKey to the attacker's value for the victim; then submit the cross-site form with the matching token. The transition succeeds because the token-cookie pair is internally consistent but belongs to the attacker, so the server cannot tell it was not issued to the victim. State transition: attacker obtains csrfKey and token -> injects csrfKey into victim -> cross-site form sends token -> pair validates -> state changed. Variants include csrfKey cookie injection, token-cookie pair from another account, sibling-domain cookie overwrite, and cookie set via CRLF. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: send a top-level cross-site GET with _method=POST and the desired parameters. Precondition: the state-changing endpoint is POST-only but honors a method override parameter. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm the change-email request has no CSRF token; then convert it to GET and add _method=POST; then verify the GET performs the change; then deliver a top-level link or redirect to the victim. The transition succeeds because Lax permits cookies on top-level GET navigations, and the override turns the GET into the protected POST. State transition: victim clicks link -> top-level GET carries Lax cookie -> override dispatches POST handler -> email changed. Variants include _method override, X-HTTP-Method-Override header, GET with a POST body, and method override in the query string. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: frame the account page and overlay two decoy buttons positioned over the delete and confirm controls. Precondition: the target action requires multiple clicks and the pages can be embedded in an attacker iframe. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm the account page can be framed; then map the delete and confirmation button positions; then build an overlay with two sequential decoys; then deliver the page and verify the action. The transition succeeds because each click is individually plausible, and the attacker controls the visual context for both. State transition: victim visits page -> first decoy click opens confirmation -> second decoy click confirms -> account deleted. Variants include two-step delete, delete plus confirmation dialog, permission grant plus confirm, and payment plus confirm. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: append a static extension to an authenticated path, have the victim request it, then fetch the cached response. Precondition: the cache applies extension-based rules and the origin ignores extra path segments. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm the origin ignores path segments after /my-account; then add a .js extension and check for cache headers; then deliver the URL to the victim; then request the same URL and read the cached account data. The transition succeeds because the cache treats the response as static while the origin serves private account data. State transition: victim requests /my-account/x.js -> origin returns account data -> cache stores it -> attacker fetches same URL -> private data disclosed. Variants include path segment ignored by origin, static extension rule, cache key without cookies, and CDN rule based on suffix. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: intercept a WebSocket chat frame, replace the encoded payload with raw HTML, and let the agent render it. Precondition: the application uses WebSockets for chat and renders incoming messages in another user's browser. The attacker drives the workflow through send a benign chat message and locate the WebSocket frame; then confirm the client encodes angle brackets; then intercept and replace the frame with an HTML event payload; then wait for the support agent to view the message. The transition succeeds because the server accepts frames that did not pass through the client encoder and stores them for rendering. State transition: attacker sends raw frame -> server stores message -> agent browser renders unencoded HTML -> script executes. Variants include stored XSS in chat, DOM XSS in message rendering, and script execution in an admin support console. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: frame the account page with the attacker's email prefilled and overlay a decoy button over the update control. Precondition: the account page is frameable and the email field accepts a URL parameter that prepopulates it. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm the account page lacks frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options; then check that the email parameter prepopulates the field; then build an iframe with the attacker email and a decoy button aligned over update; then deliver the page and verify the email change. The transition succeeds because the click is genuine and carries the valid token, so the request is authorised while the user believes they clicked an unrelated decoy. State transition: victim visits page -> iframe loads account form with attacker email -> decoy click lands on update -> email changed -> reset completes takeover. Variants include prefilled email, prefilled password change, prefilled MFA disable, and transparent overlay with variable opacity. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: send two Host headers with a cache-buster, confirm the second is reflected into a script URL, then let the poisoned response cache. Precondition: the application sits behind a cache and a front-end that validate Host inconsistently. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm that a modified single Host header is rejected; then add a second Host header with an attacker value and a cache buster; then observe the value reflected in an absolute script URL; then remove the cache buster and confirm the poisoned response is served as a cache hit. The transition succeeds because the cache and the back-end disagree about which Host value to use, so the injected value enters the cached body. State transition: request with duplicate Host -> front-end validates first -> back-end reflects second -> response cached -> victim receives poisoned page. Variants include duplicate Host, X-Forwarded-Host versus Host disagreement, absolute-URI routing, and unkeyed query or cookie inputs. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.
