text: Attack pattern: append a delimiter such as ? or ; after /my-account so the origin serves the account page while the cache stores it as static. Precondition: the account page is reachable at a path the origin truncates, and a cache applies static-extension or directory rules. The attacker drives the workflow through confirm /my-account returns the victim's API key; then test appended segments and delimiter characters against the origin; then identify the delimiter that still returns the account page and shows cache headers; then deliver the URL to the victim and fetch it unauthenticated. The transition succeeds because the two components normalise the path differently, so a private response is cached under a public-looking key. State transition: victim requests /my-account?x.js -> origin serves API key -> cache stores response -> attacker requests same URL -> key disclosed. Variants include question-mark delimiter, semicolon path parameter, encoded dot segments, and static-extension cache rules. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: change the username to administrator and the access token from a string to the integer 0. Precondition: the application stores its session as a serialized object in a cookie and compares the token loosely. The attacker drives the workflow through log in and decode the session cookie to reveal the serialized object; then change the username and adjust the string length prefix; then replace the token string with i:0 and remove its quotes; then replay the cookie and confirm the admin panel is reachable. The transition succeeds because PHP's loose comparison treats 0 as equal to a non-numeric string, so the token check passes without knowing the token. State transition: own session captured -> object edited -> username changed and token retyped to integer 0 -> loose check passes -> admin session. Variants include string-to-integer retyping, boolean coercion, null token, array wrapping, and length-prefix manipulation. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: place a break-out payload in the unkeyed cookie and replay until the poisoned response is cached. Precondition: the application reflects a cookie into the page and the cache ignores that cookie. The attacker drives the workflow through note the fehost cookie set on the home page; then confirm its value is reflected in the response body; then break out of the JavaScript string with a crafted cookie value; then replay with a cache buster, then confirm the payload is served from cache. The transition succeeds because the cache stores one response for all users while the body depends on a per-user input. State transition: payload placed in cookie -> reflected into cached body -> response cached -> victim loads page -> script executes. Variants include unkeyed cookie, unkeyed header, unkeyed query parameter, and parameter cloaking. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: send a change-address request containing __proto__ with isAdmin true, then load the admin panel. Precondition: the application performs a recursive merge of user-controlled JSON and reads authorization flags from object properties. The attacker drives the workflow through capture the change-address request and confirm the JSON response reflects the user object; then add __proto__ with a benign property and observe it inherited in the response; then pollute __proto__ with isAdmin true; then request the admin panel and delete the target user. The transition succeeds because the merge writes onto Object.prototype, so every object without its own isAdmin inherits the attacker's value. State transition: account page loaded -> __proto__ merged into prototype -> isAdmin inherited as true -> admin route authorized -> destructive action. Variants include isAdmin pollution, role pollution, feature-flag pollution, and prototype pollution reached through a nested config object. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: enumerate valid usernames from the signup error, brute-force the passwords, redirect a victim's reset link to an attacker mailbox, then edit the session cookie. Precondition: the application exposes signup, login, password reset, and cookie-based sessions. The attacker drives the workflow through send signup requests with a wordlist and filter on the 'username already exists' message; then brute-force the confirmed usernames against the login endpoint with a common password list; then request a reset for the victim while supplying the attacker's recovery address; then capture the reset link from the attacker mailbox and set a new password; then decode and edit the session cookie to escalate the logged-in or admin flag. The transition succeeds because no single control is missing catastrophically; instead each flow leaks or trusts a value that the next flow consumes. State transition: username list built -> password found -> victim reset requested with attacker email -> reset link delivered to attacker -> session cookie forged or replayed -> victim account accessed. Variants include enumeration through signup, login, or reset; password spraying after enumeration; reset-link redirection to an attacker mailbox; base64 or hash-based cookie tampering. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: keep the victim's email in the reset URL while posting the attacker's recovery email in the form body. Precondition: the reset form is reachable with the target account in the query string and the recovery address in the body. The attacker drives the workflow through open the reset page with the victim's email in the query string; then submit the form with the attacker's address in the email field; then retrieve the reset link from the attacker's own account or inbox; then set a new victim password and log in; then decode the session cookie, change the admin or user field, and re-encode it. The transition succeeds because two sources of truth for the same field exist, and the security-relevant binding uses the attacker-controlled one. State transition: reset page opened with victim email -> body posts attacker email -> token issued for victim but delivered to attacker -> password reset -> account takeover. Variants include GET versus POST precedence, duplicated body parameters, hidden fields overriding visible ones, and base64 JSON cookies with a role flag. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: read verbose API errors, exercise the outdated component, recover the embedded key, and call the mobile-only endpoint from a desktop client. Precondition: the application is deployed with default configuration and exposes APIs to untrusted clients. The attacker drives the workflow through enumerate the exposed API and read error bodies for internal paths and traces; then identify dependency versions and test the outdated component's known behaviour; then inspect client JavaScript for embedded keys and cipher modes; then replay mobile requests with a desktop User-Agent to bypass the device assumption. The transition succeeds because the security model is encoded in assumptions about the environment and the client rather than enforced by the server. State transition: verbose error discloses internals -> component or key weakness exploited -> client-assumption bypassed -> protected data or function reached. Variants include verbose stack traces, public storage buckets, unknown dependency versions, AES-ECB with a hard-coded key, and User-Agent-gated APIs. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: enumerate API paths, post to the processing endpoint, reuse the embedded decryption script, and read private message endpoints directly. Precondition: the application exposes user, processing, and messaging APIs to any HTTP client. The attacker drives the workflow through run directory discovery against /api, /api/users, and /api/messages; then read verbose responses from the user-management API; then send a POST to the processing endpoint to trigger the outdated component; then extract the key and cipher mode from decrypt.js and reproduce the decryption; then request another user's message endpoint directly. The transition succeeds because controls live in the interface or in unverified assumptions, so direct API use reaches the same functionality without them. State transition: API enumerated -> verbose response or old component leaks data -> embedded key decrypts protected file -> private messages fetched by direct endpoint access. Variants include verbose trace leakage, vulnerable utility imports, client-side decryption with a shipped key, and undocumented admin or message routes. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: change identifiers, replay workflows out of order, tamper with prices, and send boundary inputs to observe whether the server re-checks the business rule. Precondition: the application exposes user-specific resources and multi-step workflows such as checkout, recovery, and role management. The attacker drives the workflow through map every function and the identifier it accepts; then change object identifiers and replay with a lower-privilege session; then tamper with price, quantity, and currency in the checkout request; then send null, negative, and oversized values to exception paths and observe fail-open behaviour. The transition succeeds because the control exists in the happy path or in the presentation layer, and the tested request takes the path around it. State transition: legitimate request captured -> identifier, price, or sequence altered -> server applies the change without re-validating -> unauthorised state persists. Variants include IDOR on object identifiers, admin route without a check, client-side price validation, reusable reset token, and fail-open exception handler. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: perform business-logic abuse with well-formed requests and observe whether the WAF logs or blocks anything. Precondition: the application sits behind a signature-based WAF and exposes object identifiers or price fields. The attacker drives the workflow through fingerprint the WAF through headers and behaviour; then send an IDOR request that changes only an object identifier; then tamper with a price parameter and replay a state-changing request; then check WAF logs and dashboards for any detection. The transition succeeds because the WAF evaluates payload shape, not whether the principal is entitled to the object or the amount. State transition: benign-looking request -> WAF rule set finds no signature -> request forwarded -> business rule violated at the application layer. Variants include IDOR identifier increment, admin path access, price parameter change, coupon replay, and race-condition duplication. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.

text: Attack pattern: decode the serialised cookie, change the subscription or role property, re-encode it, and replay it. Precondition: the application serialises a user or note object into a cookie or hidden field. The attacker drives the workflow through identify the serialised cookie and decode it from base64; then map the object's properties and the one that gates the paid feature; then edit the property, fix the length prefixes, and re-encode; then replay the cookie and access the restricted feature; then attempt object injection with a known gadget chain where a suitable class exists. The transition succeeds because object state that drives authorisation is reconstructed from client data without integrity checks or class allowlisting. State transition: serialised cookie issued -> attacker edits isSubscribed or role -> deserialisation trusts values -> paid feature unlocked or gadget chain executed. Variants include PHP object property tampering, Python pickle payloads, Java serialised streams, .NET BinaryFormatter, and Ruby Marshal objects. The attacker repeats the sequence across accounts, tenants, or time windows until the discrepancy becomes a systematic advantage rather than a single anomaly.
